prompt: Write a novel about a teenage heroine who grows up and ends up changing the world

outline.name: Undertow
outline.description: Elara Voss, sixteen and blank, wakes in the water-stained Undertow beneath the floating city of Aethon. She collects rainwater and scavenges copper while Dreamfield coils hum in the walls, siphoning the memories of her sleeping neighbors to the rich above. She keeps her mother's last breath stored in a private place no machine can reach, and believes her emptiness makes her worthless.

outline.name: Aethon Above
outline.description: Elara climbs through a vent to watch a memory barge ascend from the Undertow to the cloud-piercing spires of Aethon. She sees how the wealthy consume the pasts of the poor, and hears the official story of the Great Forgetting. She understands that a person's life story can be bought and sold, and that her blankness makes her invisible rather than free.

outline.name: The Tithe
outline.description: Enforcers take a neighbor's daughter to be harvested under the high-tithe system. When the girl returns hollow-eyed and emptied of her childhood, Elara burns with anger but does nothing; blankness keeps her safe. She dreams of a different world, unaware that the dying revolutionary Corvin Ash is about to rewrite her fate.

outline.name: The Drowned Prayer-Fields
outline.description: Elara scavenges in the flooded prayer-fields beneath the Undertow when a body crashes through a maintenance grate. She recognizes the old man as Corvin Ash, a heretic who has been only a whisper in the Undertow for twenty years. She drags him behind a ruined altar as Enforcer light sweeps overhead.

outline.name: Corvin Ash
outline.description: Corvin presses a cold bolt to Elara's temple and tells her she was built to hold what no ordinary mind can survive. He transfers the forbidden archive—the life-memories of ten thousand erased people—into her blankness. He dies with a faint smile, leaving her with the world's greatest secret and no time to mourn.

outline.name: The Transfer
outline.description: The archive floods Elara's consciousness; ten thousand voices press against the inner walls of her mind but do not drown her. The Memorian Council detects the signal and sends Enforcers to scrub the Undertow. Elara runs, carrying a world she does not yet understand, driven by terror and the ghost of Corvin's last words.

outline.name: The Hunt
outline.description: Through flooded tunnels and abandoned copper shafts, Elara uses the archive's broken whispers to find passages her hunters do not know. She nearly drowns, nearly walks into an ambush, and learns that blankness makes her hard to track. Exhausted and bleeding, she collapses into a nest of scroungers.

outline.name: The Ghost Trader
outline.description: Rook, a wiry ghost trader with a childhood stripped from him, finds Elara hiding in his den. When an archive fragment surfaces and he hears a silver-voiced woman's laughter, he recognizes his mother. He chooses hope over safety and helps Elara hide from the Enforcers.

outline.name: The Memory-Smith
outline.description: Rook brings Elara to Sable Vey, a disillusioned former memory-smith who once calibrated extraction machines for the Council. Sable sees the archive's signature and hides the fugitives. She has been waiting for a cause worth her guilt, and she recognizes Elara for what she truly is: a living vault.

outline.name: What Sable Remembers
outline.description: Sable tells Elara the hidden history: Valerius the High Memorian created blanks three hundred years ago as secure vaults for forbidden knowledge, then forgot his own creation. She explains the Temenium, the lie of the Great Forgetting, and the Wasteland where dangerous memories are dumped. Elara's defect is a purpose.

outline.name: The Lattice
outline.description: Sable teaches Elara to build mental compartments to keep the archive from bleeding together, but Elara's breakthrough is acceptance. She lets the ten thousand voices flow through her instead of fighting them. She accesses the archive's maps, songs, and blueprints, and for the first time understands what she carries.

outline.name: The Mother's Ghost
outline.description: Deep inside her own blank architecture, Elara discovers a memory the Council never planted and never harvested: her mother's death, a last breath warm as a hand turning into sunlight. She realizes she has never been entirely empty. This secret memory becomes the anchor that keeps her from losing herself.

outline.name: The Enforcer's Knife
outline.description: Devren, a young Enforcer from the Fringe farms, polishes his father's knife—an heirloom that predates the Great Forgetting—and receives orders to terminate the blank. He is a good soldier who dreams of a world where the knife can be passed to his own child without irony. The hunt closes in around him.

outline.name: The Freight District
outline.description: Cornered in a freight yard, Elara, Rook, and Sable face Devren's squad. Devren meets Elara's eyes and sees a possibility he has been too afraid to name. He orders his men to pursue the wrong direction, letting the crew escape. In that moment, he chooses to desert.

outline.name: Desertion
outline.description: Devren joins the crew, sabotaging Enforcer pursuit with the help of his father's knife and his knowledge of patrol patterns. The others distrust him, but he gives them a tactical edge they need. He has made his choice: he is no longer on the side of forgetting.

outline.name: The Trellis Sea
outline.description: The four cross the cable web that binds the Undertow to Aethon's belly, a vertiginous climb over an endless drop. Elara uses archived memories of pre-Forgetting climbers to guide them. Rook nearly falls; Devren catches him. Blood is shared, and the group becomes a crew.

outline.name: Aethon's Underbelly
outline.description: Inside the rich city above the clouds, the crew sees what extracted memories become: power, luxury, and manufactured souls. Sable navigates through service tunnels into the Dreamfield infrastructure. They hide in a forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium and plan their next move.

outline.name: The Remembrance Salon
outline.description: The crew infiltrates a salon where nobles buy other people's hearts. A noble pays for a farmer's love for his dying daughter, sobs in her theater-box, then forgets it by evening. Elara sees the obscenity of the system and understands the Council cannot merely be stopped—it must be unmade.

outline.name: The Face of Valerius
outline.description: Valerius appears in a flickering broadcast, a three-hundred-year-old composite of swallowed lifetimes, his face composed of everything he has eaten. He announces a purge of memory contamination, and the crew realizes he sensed the archive's presence. They are out of time.

outline.name: The Plan
outline.description: Using the archive's blueprints, Sable devises a plan to sabotage the Dreamfield coils and cripple Aethon's power grid. Elara will be the key, feeding the coils a memory-song to mask their work. They resolve to strike before dawn.

outline.name: The Dreamfield Coils
outline.description: The crew infiltrates the coil chamber deep in Aethon's hull. Elara sings a memory-song from the archive while Sable plants charges. The plan nearly succeeds until an Enforcer alarm trips; suddenly they have mere minutes instead of the hour they expected.

outline.name: Discovery
outline.description: Enforcers flood the chamber, and the crew fights through a storm of alarms and shattering crystal. Rook is wounded; Devren uses his knife to cut a path. They flee across Aethon's underbelly as the charges fail, with the full power of the Council hunting them.

outline.name: Across the Fringe
outline.description: Driven from the city, the crew crosses the Fringe farmland where Devren was born. They see the poverty that feeds the memory trade and the militia pursuing them. With no road left, they choose the one direction no one dares follow: into the Wasteland.

outline.name: The Wasteland's Edge
outline.description: The Wasteland unfurls before them, a scarred territory where discarded memories have become weather, stone, and song. Sable warns of the Weeping Stones and the Chorus, but Elara feels a strange kinship. She steps forward without fear.

outline.name: The Weeping Stones
outline.description: The crew passes through a garden of stones that weep tears with nowhere to belong. Rook and Sable are nearly unmade by the psychic residue, living other people's exiles for agonizing moments. Elara alone is untouched; the Wasteland recognizes her as kin.

outline.name: The Chorus
outline.description: Elara walks alone into the Chorus, a hive-mind of a million erased voices that can unspool a person's sanity. She offers respect instead of force and asks it to join her. The Chorus responds with a polyphonic question: what will she give them in return?

outline.name: The Song of the Discarded
outline.description: Elara learns the counter-frequency, the harmony of everything the Council tried to erase. She does not command the discarded memories; she becomes their voice. She returns to the crew with an army of forgotten stories behind her and a new plan: give the past back.

outline.name: The Voice, Not the Power
outline.description: Elara integrates the Wasteland's song, accepting that she may never be simply Elara again. Rook encounters a fragment that burns with his mother's presence, and Sable finally tells the full story of her brother. They reaffirm that Elara will not rule the archive—only return it.

outline.name: Resolve
outline.description: Before the final march, each crew member declares what they want from the new world: Sable wants atonement, Devren wants a home where his knife is not a riddle, Rook wants to remember his mother's face. Elara names the goal: reverse the architecture of forgetting.

outline.name: The Memory-Storm Rises
outline.description: The Wasteland's memories rise as a storm and move with the crew toward Aethon. Gates and patrols are swallowed by voices, and the city sees impossible weather below its clouds. Panic spreads as the storm climbs the sky toward the floating capital.

outline.name: The Coils Falter
outline.description: The memory-storm breaks across Aethon's underbelly, overwhelming the Dreamfield coils and staggering the Enforcers with returned grief and joy. The crew fights upward through chaos to reach the Temenium, knowing Valerius will not wait for them.

outline.name: The Wind-Posts
outline.description: Valerius intercepts Elara on the wind-posts above the Temenium, a cathedral of stolen memory. Sable, Devren, and Rook hold off his guards below while Elara faces the High Memorian alone. He does not attack; he offers her a gift.

outline.name: The Bargain
outline.description: Valerius offers to build Elara a fabricated life: a childhood in the sun, a mother who never died, a first love, a future of luxury. It is a gentle lie, and for a moment she feels its pull. She refuses, telling him she does not want a given past—she wants a future.

outline.name: The Hollow Gaze at Last
outline.description: Enraged, Valerius drives an extraction blade into Elara's temple and tries to drink the archive. She no longer holds it; she is it. A million raw memories pour into him—the true Great Forgetting, his mother's lullaby, the weight of every stolen soul. He breaks, not into death but into the blankness he imposed on others.

outline.name: The Temenium
outline.description: Elara reaches the Temenium's core, the crystal heart of the world's stolen pasts. She sings the Wasteland's counter-frequency into it, reversing the fundamental instruction from take to return. The great machine begins to give back everything it has devoured.

outline.name: The Descent
outline.description: Stolen memories flow through every Dreamfield coil, returning to their owners across Aethon and the Undertow. A woman wakes with her grandmother's wedding, a boy finds a bear he lost ten years ago, and the rich wake with their borrowed lives gone. Aethon descends like a ship coming to harbor, sky and slum becoming one city.

outline.name: The Guild of Stewards
outline.description: In the aftermath, Sable establishes the Guild of Mnemonic Stewards to guide the return of memories, turning coercion into voluntary consent. Chaos remains, but for the first time the exchange of memory is a choice. Sable finds peace in doing for others what her brother was never allowed to choose.

outline.name: The Knife Remembers
outline.description: Devren leads a peacekeeping force made of former Enforcers who have accepted their own histories. A returned memory reveals the true story of his father's knife: a Fringe family's heirloom, not a weapon of conquest. He can pass it to the future without shame.

outline.name: The Silver-Voiced Woman
outline.description: Rook follows the returned memories to a woman singing in a market square. She has a silver voice and a mother's fierce hope, and she has been searching for him for years. They hold each other. He still cannot remember his early childhood, but he no longer needs to: he has found his beginning.

outline.name: Enough
outline.description: Elara walks into the first morning of the new city. She has given back the archive; she is blank again, but no longer empty. In her mind remains the one memory that has always been hers—her mother's last breath, warm as a hand, turning into sunlight. It is enough. It was always enough.

chapters.name: Undertow
chapters.content:
The water woke her first, as it always did. One cold thread found the crack in the ceiling beam above her cot and fell with a sound like a struck bell, a single note, over and over, telling the dark what time it was. Elara Voss opened her eyes and lay still under her blanket of salvaged sailcloth, listening to the Undertow turn slowly toward morning.

Her home was a drainage alcove some forgotten engineer had built wide and deep, a pocket of brick and rust in the underbelly of the floating city of Aethon. The ceiling bowed above her, water-stained into the shapes of continents that redrew themselves with every season of rain. Copper pipes ran the walls like veins, cold at this hour, before the coils woke. By the slit of grimy light that passed for a window, her sieve-catchment chattered faintly, sifting the condensation weeping down the hull glass. Last night's harvest: nearly two liters, clean and mineral-bright, water that had traveled through the city's bones. She counted it a good night.

Sixteen years old, and her whole fortune was rain, copper, and a heart-shaped emptiness.

Elara rose. Her joints popped in the damp the way old timber did, and she thought, as she often did, that she had been born with the bones of a much older woman. She dressed in the dark by feel — trousers patched at both knees, a vest of rubberized cloth that kept the worst of the wet off her chest — and hung her catch-bag by the door. The routine was as fixed as the fall of water: check the sieve, bank the day's drinking water in the stone cistern her mother had built, then climb the maintenance ladder to the conduit levels and hunt copper before the Enforcers' morning patrols made the lower tunnels dangerous.

Below the window, the Undertow spread out like the bottom of a boat that had forgotten it was afloat: a district of ten thousand water-stained rooms pressed against the underside of Aethon's hull, roofed by the city's own floor, floored by the black sea that breathed far below. Everything here was borrowed from above. Its light leaked down through vents and gratings, its warmth came secondhand through the pipes, its wealth fell as garbage and was caught. The people of the Undertow were the ballast of the sky-city, and they knew it. They traded in the only currency they had left: what they remembered.

Elara had nothing to trade. She had been born blank.

She knew the word the way she knew the sound of the coils at night — a fact of the world, hummed into her long before she could name it. Blank. On the file the Enforcers kept on her, stamped when she was ten, it read NULL in block letters, followed by a row of zeroes where other children's futures had been written. They had come for her the year all the Undertow children were tested, men and women in grey with plates that glowed and needles that drank. They had pressed the plate to her forehead and waited. They had frowned. They had tried again. And then they had stamped her file and gone, and no one had ever come back for her, because there was nothing in her to take.

That was the whole truth of it. Other people's minds were accounts — ledgers of everything they had seen and loved and lost, growing interest every night. The Dreamfield coils drank a little from everyone who slept, skimming the richest memories off the surface of the Undertow's dreams and sending them up through the walls to the cloud-piercing spires of Aethon, where the wealthy paid fortunes to live a day as a fisherman's son, or to feel a mother's grief they had never earned, or to remember a childhood of sun. Elara had heard the rich called the *consumers* in a voice that made it sound like a disease. Down here, they were simply *above*. And above had an appetite that never ended.

Elara's account was empty. The coils sang over her sleeping body at the hour of the pull and found nothing to skim — no first kiss, no dead grandmother's recipe, no terror, no joy. The machines passed her by like water over a stone. Once, that had seemed like freedom. Her neighbors paid their memories in sleep, waking each morning with holes in themselves they could not quite name, and Elara woke whole and untouched, and she had told herself for years that this made her lucky.

She knew better now. Luck was something you could spend. She was not lucky; she was worthless — the one thing in all the Undertow that even the thieves above had no use for.

She climbed the ladder to the conduit levels and worked until her fingers were green with verdigris and her bag was heavy with stripped wire. The copper came from dead lines, conduits the city had abandoned when the Dreamfield was laid, a generation of plumbing that predated the coils and so escaped their hungry hum. She knew the good spots the way she knew her own breathing: the collapsed gallery off Level Nine where a pipe had burst and drowned three corridors and left the copper gleaming in the murk; the ventilator shaft behind the old pump room where the wire hung like Spanish moss. Copper was the only thing that still loved her hands. It came away from the walls willingly, warm from the earth-heat of the hull, and at the scrounger market it bought her bread, lamp-oil, and, twice a month, a real egg.

She was hauling a coil of wire through a flooded junction when she heard Sila singing.

It came from the next room over, thin and cracked as old lacquer: a song Elara had heard a hundred times and could never quite catch the tune of, because Sila herself could never quite remember it. Sila was sixty-three and had once been a singer in the upper districts — or so she insisted, in the mornings, before the forgetting set in. She had performed before Memorian Council patrons in a hall of glass. She had been paid in gold. She had been adored. Then the high-tithe collectors had come for her, as they came for everyone eventually, and her voice, her songs, her audience, her whole bright history had been harvested in one long terrible night, and the woman who woke in the morning was a husk with a silver tongue and nothing in her head but splinters.

Every night the coils took what was left. Every morning Sila hummed the ghost of a song she could no longer remember having written, and Elara stood in the flooded junction and listened, and hated the walls with a clean, useless hate.

"Elara," Sila said when she emerged, blinking in the grey light that fell through a grate in the ceiling. She was wrapped in a shawl of unraveling wool, her eyes the pale blue of water that had forgotten the sky. "I had a dream. There was a garden. Do you think I ever had a garden?"

Elara thought of the copper in her bag, the bread it would buy, the fact that Sila's garden — if it had ever existed — was now being worn by some noblewoman three miles above them like a borrowed scarf. "I don't know," she said.

"No," Sila agreed, without sadness. Sadness required a memory to be sad about, and the coils had eaten hers. "But it's nice to think so." She shuffled past, humming, and Elara watched her go and felt the hate turn over in her chest like something alive.

She should have said something. She never did. Blankness kept her safe. The Enforcers didn't watch her because there was nothing in her worth watching, and she had learned to move through the world as a shadow of a shadow, asking no questions, making no friends, collecting rain and copper and nothing else. To speak, to act, to matter — those were things for people with pasts, people with weight. A blank could not afford them. A blank did not exist, and the only power that came from not existing was that no one thought to destroy you.

That evening, she sat in her alcove as the Undertow dimmed, eating bread and the last of yesterday's soup while the light from the gratings above faded from grey to grey. Below her window the lamps of the lower streets guttered on, one by one, and the city's long exhale began. Doors closed. Voices softened. Children were tucked into beds where the coils would find them, and their parents kissed their foreheads with a tenderness that would be skimmed off before dawn and sold.

At the hour of the pull, the walls began to hum.

Elara lay on her cot with her eyes open, as she did every night, because there was no point pretending to sleep. The hum rose from the copper veins in the walls — a deep, chorded sound, almost beautiful, like the memory of a cello underwater. It swelled until the water in her cistern trembled and the dust motes danced in the grimy light, and then it settled into the long, patient drone of something feeding. Through the wall, she heard the child next door cry out in her sleep — a name, a lost thing, a word the coils were already carrying away — and then go quiet, and Sila's humming stop mid-note, cut off like a thread.

The coils fed for an hour. Elara lay under her sailcloth blanket and did not dream, because she had nothing to dream about. The hum passed over her like wind over a stone.

When it faded, and the Undertow's slow breathing resumed, she let herself go to the one place the machines had never found.

It was not a place she could describe, even to herself — not a room, exactly, not a memory. It was more like a pocket sewn into the inside of her, a fold of blankness where the coils' reach had never gone. She had discovered it the night her mother died, two years ago, in this same alcove, on this same cot.

The damp had taken her mother slowly, the way it took everyone down here who lived long enough — the lung-rot that came with the water, that turned breath into a labor and sleep into a drowning. Elara had been fourteen, and she had sat at the bedside for three days holding her mother's hand while the woman's chest worked like a bellows full of sand. The coil hum had risen that night as it always did, and her mother, still conscious, still herself in the last hour the coils would allow, had turned her head on the pillow and looked at Elara with eyes that were suddenly, terribly clear.

"Remember me," she had whispered. It was the cruelest thing anyone had ever said to Elara — a command to do the one thing she was built unable to do, to hold in her empty head the shape of the only person who had ever loved her. She had opened her mouth to apologize, to explain that she was blank, that she would try, that she would try so hard—

And then her mother's hand had tightened, and her mother's breath had come out in one long, final rush, warm against Elara's cheek, and Elara had taken it in without meaning to, breathing her mother's last breath into the deepest part of herself.

And there, in the fold the machines had never mapped, something had caught. Not a story. Not a picture. Just a warmth, and a pressure like a hand, and a sense of light the color of honey. Her mother's last breath, kept like a coal in a hearth that should have been empty. The only memory Elara Voss had ever owned, hidden in the one place in the world no machine could reach.

She visited it now, as she did every night after the pull, when the coils were full and sleeping. She cupped it in the dark of herself the way her mother had once cupped her face, and it glowed there, small and stubborn, a warmth that had nothing to do with the city's stolen heat. It was not enough to make her worth anything. It was not enough to trade, or to matter, or to give her the weight the world required. But it was hers, and as long as she could feel it burning in the fold of her blankness, she was not entirely empty.

It is enough, she told herself, the way she told herself every night. It is enough. It is enough.

It never felt like enough.

She was on the roof of the Undertow when she saw the barge — though "roof" was a generous word for the catwalk of old conduit that ran along the hull's lowest service vent, where the maintenance grates were too narrow for a man and just wide enough for a girl who had learned to be a shadow. She had come up to check the sieve-catchments after a squall, and there, through a crack in the city's floor, the night opened above her.

The barge rose from the deep-harbor lock below the Undertow, golden and immense, trailing light like a falling star dragged upward. Its hold was full of memory-cylinders, thousands of them, stacked and gleaming — the night's tithe, everything the Undertow had dreamed and lost, bound for the spires of Aethon. Elara watched it climb, watched the light of a thousand stolen lives rise away from her, and she felt something stir in the fold of her chest, a warmth that had no business waking.

She had heard that in the upper city, the rich gathered to drink these lives like wine. She had heard that a man could buy a whole childhood and wear it for an evening, and that a woman could pay to feel a love so large it broke her heart, and that they called it *living richly*, never once asking whose lives they were living. She had heard the official story, the one the Memorian Council told: that the Great Forgetting had been a mercy, that the Undertow's memories were poison and disease, that the coils were *purifying* them, saving the poor from themselves.

She did not believe it. She did not know why she did not believe it. But as the barge shrank to a point of gold against the belly of the city above, Elara Voss, sixteen years old and worth nothing at all, pressed her palm to her chest where her mother's last breath burned, and thought: *One day I will climb. One day I will see what they do with us.*

Then the light was gone, and the hum of the coils resumed, patient and hungry, and she climbed back down into the water-stained dark to count her copper and her rain, worthless and safe, exactly as the world required her to be.

She did not know, yet, that her emptiness was not a hole. She did not know it was a room — a vast, high-ceilinged room with room enough for the world's forgotten things. She only lay on her cot in the dark, listening to the water fall, believing she was nothing.

But somewhere deep in the city's walls, in a place where the coils' hum could not reach, a dying man was already walking toward a maintenance grate. And the warmth in Elara's chest burned on, patient as a kept promise, waiting for the night it would be asked to hold so much more.

set.name: Elara Voss
set.description: Sixteen-year-old girl, born blank (mind reads NULL; Enforcer file stamped with zeroes at age ten, never harvested). Lives alone in a drainage alcove beneath the floating city of Aethon, in the Undertow district. Collects rainwater via sieve-catchment into a stone cistern and scavenges copper from dead conduit lines to trade for bread and lamp-oil. Keeps her mother's last breath stored in a private fold of her mind that the Dreamfield coils cannot reach; visits it each night after the pull. Believes her emptiness makes her worthless, though she has a private resolve to one day climb into Aethon and see what the rich do with stolen memories. Physical condition: lean, damp, joints ache from the wet; wears patched trousers and a rubberized vest. Relationships: mother dead two years of lung-rot; neighbor Sila, a harvested former singer. Knowledge: Undertow geography, copper routes, coil schedules, Enforcer patrol patterns; distrusts the official story of the Great Forgetting.

set.name: Sila
set.description: Sixty-three-year-old neighbor in the Undertow, once a singer who performed before Memorian Council patrons in a hall of glass; her memories were harvested by high-tithe collectors. Now a husk with a silver tongue who hums the ghost of a song she can no longer remember writing each morning. Pale blue eyes, shawl of unraveling wool. She forgets her own past without sadness because the coils ate her sadness along with everything else.

Two years before the story begins, Elara's mother died of the lung-rot in their alcove. In her final hour she told Elara to remember her; her last breath came out warm against Elara's cheek and was taken into the deepest fold of Elara's blankness, where no machine can reach. This is the only memory Elara has ever owned.

When Elara was ten, Enforcers tested all Undertow children with memory plates; Elara's mind read NULL and her file was stamped with zeroes. No one has ever harvested her, which is why blankness keeps her safe and invisible.

Neighbor Sila, once a celebrated singer in the upper districts, was stripped of her memories by high-tithe collectors and now lives as a forgetful husk humming a forgotten song. A daily reminder of what the coils do to the Undertow.

The dying man walking through the city's walls toward a maintenance grate must reach the Undertow and crash through the grate into the flooded prayer-fields, where Elara will find and hide him from Enforcer light (Chapters 3-4).

Elara's private resolve to climb into Aethon must pay off: she climbs through a vent to watch the memory barge ascend, hears the official story of the Great Forgetting, and realizes her blankness makes her invisible rather than free (Chapter 1).

chapters.name: Aethon Above
chapters.content:
The vent was her second home, and like the first, it was too small for anyone who had ever learned to expect comfort.

Elara Voss lay on her back in the maintenance duct that ran along the Undertow's ceiling, her catch-bag pressed flat beneath her spine, her patched knees bent to fit the curve of the pipe. Above her, through a grid of rust-softened bars, the floor of the world gave way to open air. She had found this place three years ago, chasing a leak that had drowned a whole corridor of copper, and she had kept it secret ever since — a thief's perch, a spy's roost, the one window in all the Undertow that looked up instead of down.

Today was the rising of the quarter-tithe barge, and the vent was packed with her own patience and the smell of old rain.

She had woken before the coils' hum had fully died, dressed in the dark, and climbed. It was a good climb — forty rungs of ladder, then a crawl through a collapsed service run where she had to hold her breath through a two-meter stretch of silt, then the vent itself, bolted from the wrong side and hanging by one good hinge. She had oiled it with lamp grease stolen from a dead pump room, a drop a month for three years, until the squeal had gone out of it like a tamed animal. Now it swung wide with a sound no louder than a sigh, and the sky poured in.

Not the sky, exactly. The sky was up there somewhere, beyond the cloud-piercing spires of Aethon. What poured into the vent was Aethon's belly — the vast under-structure of the floating city, a continent of hull-plating and cable and machinery hanging in the dark like the underside of a whale. Light leaked down from its seams in slow gold rivers. From this angle, the city above was not a city at all but a ceiling, and Elara was a girl lying on the wrong side of it, looking up at a world that had built itself out of other people's lives.

The barge came on time.

She felt it before she saw it: a change in the air pressure, a thickening of the hum that never quite stopped even in daylight, the Dreamfield coils in the walls picking up the harmonics of something enormous approaching. Then the deep-harbor lock below the Undertow opened its great doors with a sound like a cathedral clearing its throat, and the barge rose.

It was golden. It was always golden. A memory barge rode on the light of what it carried, and what it carried was the tithe — three months of the Undertow's harvested lives, distilled and sealed in thousands of memory-cylinders stacked in its hold like amber bottles in a wine cellar. The barge rose past her vent, so close she could have reached out and touched the enameled hull if she had dared, and Elara held her breath and watched the faces of the people on it.

There were only three. A pilot at the prow, wearing the grey of the Memorian Council's civil service, his face smooth and bored, a man who had made this ascent a thousand times and no longer saw the cargo. A guard with a shock-rifle cradled in his arms, his eyes scanning the Undertow's rooftops with the professional blankness of a man paid not to think. And a woman.

The woman stood at the stern rail, and she was the reason Elara came.

She was not young. Her hair was the color of ash, and her shoulders had the stoop of a life spent bent over ledgers. But her eyes were bright and hungry, and she carried a small brass device in her hand — a reader, Elara knew, though she had never seen one this close — and as the barge climbed, she held the reader out over the rail and let it drink the light of the hold below.

That was the part Elara could never look away from. The woman was tasting. Not food, not wine. The barge's hold was full of the Undertow's pasts, and the woman stood above it like a sommelier above a cellar, lifting the reader to her lips, pressing a stud, and letting a memory flow into her — a few seconds of someone else's life, drawn up through the device and into her own head.

Elara watched the woman's face change as it happened. There was a girl in the Undertow — Marit, from the weavers' block, nineteen years old, with a laugh like a struck bell — and somewhere in the barge's hold was the memory of Marit's mother teaching her to spin wool in the light of a shuttered lamp. The woman on the barge found it. Elara could not hear it, could not see it, but she saw the woman's lips part and her eyes soften and her shoulders drop, and she knew the woman was wearing Marit's mother's voice like a coat, feeling the rough wool between her fingers, standing in a lamplit room that had never been hers.

The reader clicked. The woman's face smoothed again, the softness draining out of it as the memory was spent — consumed, used up, gone. She frowned, tapped the reader, and reached for another cylinder.

Elara's hands made fists against the vent floor.

That was the whole of it, the entire architecture of the world made visible: a woman three hundred meters above her tasting the only warm thing a girl below had ever owned, swallowing it in three seconds flat, and moving on. The coils skimmed the Undertow's dreams every night, sure — but that was the slow harvest, the tax. This was the high-tithe barge, the quarterly wholesale. Everything the coils had gathered, everything the collectors had taken by force from people like Sila, bound up in gold and carried to the spires to be drunk like wine and spent like money.

And in the spires, in the halls Elara could not see and could only imagine, there were people for whom this was a living — real living, the only kind that counted. She had heard the stories, passed down the Undertow in whispers, each telling more ornate than the last. A nobleman in a theater-box paying a fortune to weep over a dead fisherman's grief, sobbing into his gloves, moved by a love he had never earned, then forgetting it entirely by the time the lamps were lit. A lady of the Council buying a childhood of sun and riverbanks and wearing it for an afternoon, returning it empty. They called it living richly. They called the Undertow's memories the spice of Aethon, and they ate and ate, and the Undertow grew dimmer by the mouthful.

Elara pressed her cheek against the vent bars and watched the barge shrink against the city's belly, and a thought rose in her, cold and clear as the water in her cistern: a person's whole life could be bought and sold.

Not a metaphor. Not a figure of speech. Literally. Her mother's face could be in that hold. Sila's garden could be in that hold. Marit's laugh could be in that hold, being tasted right now by an ash-haired woman with a brass reader, and when it was gone there would be nothing left of it anywhere in the world except the ghost of a tune Sila could not remember.

She had known this. Everyone in the Undertow knew this, the way everyone knows the tide will come in. But knowing a thing and seeing it were different animals, and seeing it from this close, in this much detail, felt like being shown the inside of her own chest.

Then the barge's loudspeaker crackled, and the official story began.

It was the same recording every quarter, looped for the benefit of anyone below who cared to listen, and Elara had heard it so many times she could have recited it in her sleep. But today, with the gold light of the hold still stinging her eyes, she listened as if for the first time.

"CITIZENS OF THE UNDERTERRANEAN DISTRICTS," the voice said, amplified until it rang off the hull-plating and made the coils in the walls hum in sympathy. It was a man's voice, warm and paternal, the voice of a man who had never been cold or hungry or afraid, telling the cold and hungry and afraid that everything was being done for them. "THE MEMORIAN COUNCIL GREETS YOU. WE RISE TODAY ON THE WINGS OF THE QUARTER-TITHE, A HARVEST OF GENEROSITY FROM THE DEEP DISTRICTS TO THE LAMPS OF THE HIGH CITY. REMEMBER: THE GREAT FORGETTING WAS A GIFT."

The barge kept climbing. The voice kept talking.

"BEFORE THE FORGETTING, THE WORLD WAS SICK. THE OLD WORLD KEPT EVERY MEMORY, AND THE MEMORIES WERE POISON. THEY FESTERED. THEY TURNED NEIGHBOR AGAINST NEIGHBOR. THEY CARRIED WARS ACROSS GENERATIONS, BECAUSE A MAN WHO REMEMBERS A GRIEF WILL PASS THAT GRIEF TO HIS SON, AND HIS SON TO HIS SON, AND THE GRIEF BECOMES A DUTY AND THE DUTY BECOMES A BLADE. THE COUNCIL SAW THIS AND SAID: ENOUGH. WE WILL TAKE THE POISON OUT OF THE BLOOD. WE WILL DRAW THE SICK MEMORIES UP INTO THE CLEAN AIR OF AETHON, WHERE THEY CAN BE PURIFIED IN THE LIGHT OF THE TEMENIUM, AND WE WILL GIVE THE PEOPLE OF THE DEEP DISTRICTS PEACE."

Purified, Elara thought, watching the ash-haired woman lift another cylinder to her lips. That's what we call it now. Purified. Like dirty water. Like a wound.

"DO NOT GRIEVE FOR WHAT YOU HAVE GIVEN," the voice continued, warming to its work. "WHAT YOU HAVE GIVEN IS HEALED. WHAT YOU HAVE GIVEN IS KEPT SAFE IN THE VAULTS OF THE TEMENIUM, THE GREAT MEMORY OF THE WORLD, WHERE NOTHING IS EVER TRULY LOST. THE COILS DO NOT STEAL. THEY CARRY. THEY CARRY YOUR LIVES UP TO THE LIGHT, WHERE THE COUNCIL GUARDS THEM FOR ETERNITY, SO THAT THE PAST MAY NEVER AGAIN HARM THE FUTURE. THIS IS THE GREAT FORGETTING. THIS IS YOUR SALVATION. THIS IS—"

Elara stopped listening. The words had always made her stomach turn, but today they made her want to scream, and screaming was a luxury a blank could not afford.

Because here was the trap in the official story, the hinge it all swung on: the Council claimed the memories were poison. They claimed to be taking them for the people's own good, to heal them, to purify them, to guard them. And if you believed that — if you believed your past was a disease and the coils a cure — then the high-tithe barge was an ambulance, the ash-haired woman a healer, the Temenium a hospital, and the people of the Undertow the fortunate sick.

But Elara had watched the woman taste a weaver girl's mother like wine. You did not drink a cure. You did not spend a medicine on a theater-box, weeping and forgetting it by evening. The Council's tongue did not fit the Council's teeth, and she had known it since she was old enough to know anything at all.

What she had never been able to work out — what she turned over in the dark of her alcove night after night, the way you worry a loose tooth — was why the official story bothered her at all. A blank had no stake in it. A blank had no memories for the coils to take, no past for the barge to carry, no grief to be purified. If the Great Forgetting was a theft, she was not among the robbed. If it was a mercy, she was the one person it had already, completely, mercifully emptied.

She had told herself, for years, that this made her free.

The barge was small now, a golden mote climbing the last stretch of cable toward the lowest spires. Elara watched it go, and she felt the old comfortable lie crumble in her hands.

Free. That was the lie. Blankness had never been freedom; it had been invisibility, and invisibility was only freedom if you wanted to be seen by no one, touched by no one, remembered by no one. The people on the barge were being robbed, yes — but they were being robbed of something. They had weight. They had lives that were worth stealing. Even the ash-haired woman, whose face Elara hated with a clean, quiet hate, had chosen that face from somewhere, had a history that had made her hungry, had a past that had shaped her into a woman who could stand on a barge and drink a stranger's mother.

Elara had nothing shaped. Nothing had ever shaped her. The coils passed over her like wind over a stone, and the Enforcers had stamped her file NULL and walked away, and she had told herself that the reason they left her alone was safety — but the truth, the ugly truth she had been circling for years, was that they left her alone because there was nothing to want.

She was not invisible. Invisibility was a trick, a skill, a cloak you could take off. She was transparent. She was the glass the world looked through without seeing, and what she had mistaken for freedom was simply the absence of being wanted.

The barge vanished into the belly of the spires. The loudspeaker fell silent. The coils in the walls settled back into their low, patient drone, and the Undertow went on being the Undertow: water dripping, lamps guttering, a child crying somewhere below, Sila's voice rising thin and cracked from the weavers' block — humming, always humming, the ghost of a song that no longer existed anywhere except in the throat of a woman who had forgotten writing it.

And Elara lay in the vent with her cheek against the rusted bars, and watched the place where the gold light had been, and felt something settle in her chest like a stone coming to rest at the bottom of a well.

It was not anger. She had carried anger for years, and it had done nothing but wear grooves in her. It was not even sorrow. It was understanding — the cold, clean click of a lock opening — and what it showed her was this: a person's life story could be bought and sold. She had seen it with her own eyes, watched a woman drink a girl's mother in three seconds flat. And her own life story, such as it was, was worth nothing at all to anyone — not because she was safe, and not because she was free, but because she was empty.

She had always thought emptiness was the only thing keeping her alive. Now, for the first time, she understood what it was actually costing her.

There was a warmth in the fold of her chest, the one place the machines had never reached, her mother's last breath burning patient as a coal. It was the only thing she had ever owned. It was not a story. It was not a life. It was just a warmth, a pressure like a hand, a light the color of honey — and lying in the vent, watching the last of the barge's gold fade from the sky, Elara Voss pressed her palm to her chest and thought, fiercely, that if that was all she had, she would find a way to make it worth more than everything on that barge.

She did not know how. She did not know what it would cost. She only knew that she could not lie here forever, watching other people's lives rise past her like falling stars dragged upward, tasting them with someone else's mouth, being nothing.

She would climb. Not into the vent — she had climbed that long ago. Into the city. Into the spires, the halls, the Temenium itself if she could find a way. She would see what they did with the Undertow's lives, with Sila's garden and Marit's mother and all the warm bright things the coils carried away. She would see it with her own eyes, from inside, and then she would decide what the warmth in her chest was for.

Below her, the Undertow went on dripping and humming and forgetting, and the city above went on eating, and somewhere deep in the walls — in a place where the coils' hum could not reach — a dying man walked toward a maintenance grate, his pockets full of a secret too heavy for any ordinary mind to carry.

Elara did not know that yet. She only knew she could not stay here, worthless and safe, exactly as the world required her to be.

She pushed herself backward out of the vent, swung the grate shut on its one good hinge, and climbed down into the water-stained dark, carrying nothing but rain, copper, and a warmth that burned like a promise.

And the golden light of the barge stayed behind her eyes, all the way down, and for the first time in her life she understood what it meant to want something they could never take.

set.name: Elara Voss
set.description: Sixteen-year-old girl, born blank (mind reads NULL; Enforcer file stamped with zeroes at age ten, never harvested). Lives alone in a drainage alcove beneath the floating city of Aethon, in the Undertow district. Collects rainwater via sieve-catchment into a stone cistern and scavenges copper from dead conduit lines to trade for bread and lamp-oil. Keeps her mother's last breath stored in a private fold of her mind that the Dreamfield coils cannot reach; visits it each night after the pull. This chapter she climbed her secret maintenance vent and witnessed the quarter-tithe memory barge ascend to Aethon, saw an ash-haired Council taster with a brass reader drink a weaver girl's mother-memory from the hold, and heard the broadcast official story of the Great Forgetting. She now understands viscerally that a person's life story can be bought and sold, and that her blankness makes her invisible rather than free; she has resolved to climb into Aethon itself and see the upper city from inside. Physical condition: lean, damp, joints ache from the wet; wears patched trousers and a rubberized vest; a new cold resolve burning in her chest alongside the kept warmth. Relationships: mother dead two years of lung-rot; neighbor Sila, a harvested former singer whose ghost-song she heard again this chapter. Knowledge: Undertow geography, copper routes, coil schedules, Enforcer patrol patterns; the mechanics of the tithe barge and taster trade; distrusts the official story of the Great Forgetting.

set.name: Sila
set.description: Sixty-three-year-old neighbor of Elara in the Undertow, once a singer who performed before Memorian Council patrons in a hall of glass; her memories were harvested by high-tithe collectors. Now a husk with a silver tongue who hums the ghost of a song she can no longer remember writing each morning. Pale blue eyes, shawl of unraveling wool. She forgets her own past without sadness because the coils ate her sadness along with everything else. Unchanged by the chapter's events; her morning ghost-song reached Elara's ears as the barge rose, a reminder of what the tithe makes of the Undertow.

On the morning of the quarter-tithe rising, Elara watched from her secret maintenance vent as the golden memory barge ascended from the deep-harbor lock to Aethon's spires. An ash-haired Council taster with a brass reader drank a memory from the hold (Marit the weaver's mother teaching wool-spinning), and the loudspeaker looped the official story of the Great Forgetting. Elara concluded that a life story can be bought and sold, that blankness makes her invisible rather than free, and resolved to climb into Aethon itself and see the upper city from inside.

Elara's resolve, born while watching the barge, to climb into Aethon Proper and see the upper city from inside must eventually pay off when she physically enters the rich city above the clouds, which the crew infiltrates via service tunnels in Chapter 16 (Aethon's Underbelly).

chapters.name: The Tithe
chapters.content:
The Enforcers came on a rainless morning, which meant everyone saw them coming.

On wet days the grey patrols moved fast and ugly, heads down, and the Undertow could pretend it had not noticed them until they were already inside a door. But the sky above the gratings was pale and dry, and the light fell straight down, and by the time the first shock-rifle butt struck the weavers' block door, half the district was watching from its windows.

Elara was at the cistern when she heard the knock. Not a knock — a sound like a fist through paper, and then a woman's voice, high and breaking, and a child crying in a register that Elara's body recognized before her mind did. She set down her dipper. The water trembled in the stone and went still.

Through her window she could see them: three Enforcers in grey, standing in the narrow lane outside the weavers' block, and a fourth holding the arm of a girl. The girl was twelve. Her name was Nessa, and she was the youngest of the weaver's children, the one who ran the district's errands with her hair always coming loose, who knew every shortcut and every dog and every joke, who had once traded Elara a whole slice of bread for a coil of copper wire and refused to take the change.

Nessa was twelve, and she was crying, and the Enforcer holding her arm was doing it the way you hold a thing that means nothing: loosely, patiently, waiting for her to stop.

"Nessa," Elara whispered, to the glass, to no one.

The weaver — Nessa's mother, whose name was Onna — came out of the block door with her hands out, palms up, the old posture of the Undertow, the posture that said *I have nothing, take what you must, spare what you can*. The lead Enforcer read from a slate in a voice that carried the way loudspeakers carried, flat and amplified, meant to be heard by everyone.

"Onna Kells, weaver's block, Level Nine. By the authority of the Memorian Council and the provisions of the high-tithe, your daughter Nessa Kells is called to the collection for a full harvest of the childhood years, ages six through twelve, owed and overdue. Noncompliance is a breach of civic duty and will be met with—"

"My girl's only twelve," Onna said, and her voice was not pleading. It was the voice of someone stating a fact the universe had got wrong. "She's only twelve. The tithe is for grown ones. The tithe is for—"

"The high-tithe is assessed per household," the Enforcer said, not unkindly, the way you might explain arithmetic to a child. "Household Kells has not met its levy in three quarters. The collection stands. The child will be returned by evening, emptied of the childhood years as assessed, in full accordance with the codes of the Great Forgetting. This is your salvation, citizen. The Council does this for her own good."

Elara stood at her window with the dipper still in her hand, and she watched Nessa stop crying.

That was the worst part. Nessa did not scream, did not fight, did not look at her mother for rescue. She went quiet, the way children go quiet when the thing they feared has finally arrived and there is no point left in fearing it, and she walked with the Enforcer without being pulled. She was a good girl. She had always been a good girl. The Undertow taught its children one lesson and taught it early: when the grey come, you go, because the grey always come, and the only thing you can keep is your dignity in walking.

The door of the grey van closed. The van did not go up — the upper city was not for the likes of it. It went sideways, through the maintenance tunnels, toward the deep-harbor lock where the collection ships waited, and Elara watched it go and felt something move in her chest like a fish under ice.

She did nothing.

She stood there with the dipper dripping onto her boots, and she did nothing, and blankness kept her safe, exactly as it always had. The Enforcers did not glance at her window. There was nothing in her worth glancing at. She was transparent, the glass the world looked through, and it was the only armor she had ever owned, and she wore it now while a twelve-year-old girl was taken to have her childhood drained out of her like water from a boot.

Onna did not go back inside. She stood in the lane with her hands at her sides, and after a while she sat down on the step, and after a while longer she began to rock, very slightly, the way you rock a thing that hurts. Elara watched her for a long time through the glass, and then she put down the dipper and went back to the cistern and finished her morning work, because there was nothing else to do, because there was never anything else to do.

The Undertow went about its day. That was the true horror of it, the one the loudspeakers never mentioned: the day after the grey came was a day like any other. Water dripped. Coils hummed. Bread was baked and sold. Sila hummed her ghost-song from the weavers' block — quieter today, as if she knew, as if some splinter of her old self could still feel the shape of a child being taken — and the market opened and the copper changed hands and nobody said Nessa's name, because saying it made it real, and it was already real.

Elara worked the conduit levels until her hands were green and her bag heavy, and she did not think about Nessa. She thought about copper, about the price of bread, about the way the light fell through the gratings, about anything at all except the gray van and the quiet girl walking into it. She was very good at this. She had had years of practice. She had watched Sila be taken in pieces over a whole terrible night and said nothing, and she had told herself it was safety, and safety had become a habit, and habit had become a kind of death that let you keep breathing.

By dusk she was back in her alcove, eating bread and soup, and the Undertow was closing its shutters one by one, and she was almost able to pretend that the morning had not happened.

Then the van came back.

It came back the way it had left, sideways through the maintenance tunnels, and it stopped in the lane outside the weavers' block, and the Enforcer opened the door, and Nessa stepped out.

Elara's hand went to the glass.

Nessa was hollow-eyed. That was the word for it, hollow-eyed, and Elara had heard it all her life without understanding it, the way you hear a word for a disease you have never seen. Now she saw it. Nessa's eyes were open and looking, but there was nothing behind them, nothing at all, the way a window is behind a pane of glass — you could see through to the room, but the room was empty. Her hair had come loose, and no one had tied it back for her, and she did not tie it back herself. She walked to her mother without being pulled, the way she had walked to the van, and Onna caught her by the shoulders and said her name, and Nessa looked at her mother with those hollow eyes and said, in a small, flat voice, the first and only thing she said all evening:

"Who are you?"

Onna made a sound Elara had never heard a human being make, a sound that came from somewhere below language, and Nessa stood there in the middle of it, looking at her mother's tears the way you look at weather through a window, and after a moment she turned and went inside the block, and the door closed, and the lane was quiet.

The Enforcers drove away. The Undertow, which had been watching from its windows with a held breath, let the breath out and did not look at one another. Somewhere a woman began to cry and stopped herself. Sila's humming had stopped, and did not start again.

Elara stood at her own window with her palm pressed flat against the glass, and she felt the anger rise in her like floodwater, clean and huge and useless.

It was the clearest feeling she had ever had. It had a shape and a weight and a taste, and it was the most real thing in her body, more real than her heartbeat, more real than the cold. And it was entirely, completely useless, because what was she going to do with it? She was sixteen. She was blank. She weighed nothing in the ledger of the world. The anger sat in her chest like a coal, and the only other warmth in her was her mother's last breath, and the two burned against each other all night, and she did nothing, because doing something was a luxury she could not afford, because the grey did not come for blanks, and she had built her whole life on that, and if she threw it away on one girl's emptied eyes, what would she have left to keep anyone safe with?

Nothing, came the answer, and it was the truest thing she had ever thought. She had nothing. She was nothing. And Nessa was empty now too, and the world was full of the emptied, and the coils hummed on, and the barge would rise again in three months with more gold in its hold, and nothing would ever change, because nobody with any weight in the world wanted it to.

She slept badly that night. She lay under her sailcloth blanket and listened to the water fall and the coils feed, and when the hum finally faded she did not visit her mother's breath the way she usually did, because she was afraid that tonight, for the first time, it would not be enough.

Instead she dreamed.

Elara almost never dreamed. Blankness did not dream — or rather, it dreamed in null, in the dark behind the dark, in nothing at all. But that night, worn thin by anger and grief, she dreamed.

She dreamed of a world without the coils.

It was not a grand dream. There were no armies in it, no towers falling. She dreamed of the Undertow as it might have been: the same dripping walls, the same grimy light, but the copper veins in the walls were cold and silent, and the hum was gone. People slept in the dark and woke with their own faces. A woman woke remembering her mother's wedding and wept with joy at the remembering. A boy found a bear he had lost ten years ago, and it was exactly where he had left it. And Nessa — Nessa was twelve, and her eyes were not hollow, and she ran through the lanes with her hair coming loose, laughing at a joke that was hers to keep.

In the dream, Elara stood at her own window and watched the Undertow wake up full, and she understood, with the clarity dreams have, that the hum in the walls was a machine and a machine could be stopped, and that a stopped machine did not mean a world destroyed but a world given back.

Then the dream shifted, the way dreams do, and she was somewhere else. She was high up, higher than the vents, higher than the gratings, and below her the whole world spread out like water, and she was standing on the underside of the sky with her mother's breath burning in her chest like a lamp, and there was a sound in her ears, a sound like ten thousand voices at once, and they were all saying her name.

She woke with the word still ringing in the dark of her skull, and for a moment she could not remember her own name, only the way it had sounded when ten thousand strangers said it.

Then the water dripped, and the coils hummed, and she was Elara Voss, worthless and safe, and the dream dissolved like a breath on glass.

She sat up. Dawn was a long way off. Through the window, the Undertow was a pit of shadow, and in the pit, somewhere, Nessa was asleep or awake with nothing in her head, and Onna was holding her, and Sila was not humming.

Elara pressed her hand to her chest, where the two coals burned — the anger and the warmth — and she made herself a promise she did not know how to keep.

*One day*, she thought. *One day I will stop watching. One day the grey will come for me, or I will go for them, and I will not be nothing anymore.*

It was a child's promise, made in the dark, and she knew it. She had made promises in the dark before. But the dream had left something behind, a splinter of certainty, and she held it the way she held her mother's breath, and it kept her from falling asleep again until the coils' hum died and the grey light of morning began to leak through the gratings.

She did not know that, far above her, in the highest reaches of the city's walls, in a place the coils' hum had never touched, a dying man was even then pressing his ear to a maintenance grate and listening to the water fall below him.

She did not know his name. She did not know that he had spent twenty years walking toward this grate, carrying a secret too heavy for any ordinary mind, and that he had chosen her — her, the blank, the worthless, the nothing — because she was the only vessel in the world that could hold it without breaking.

She only sat on her cot in the grey morning, holding her mother's last breath and the splinter of her dream, and believed she was nothing, exactly as the world required her to be.

But above her, in the walls, Corvin Ash smiled a thin, tired smile, and began to pry at the grate.

And far below, in the flooded prayer-fields where the old altars drowned in their own dark water, the place the dying man was falling toward was already waiting.
