The dead cable that climbed toward the hatch was thin — thin as her thumb at the far end, sagging in a long curve between two moorings, with nothing but the cloud-sea and the far fields a thousand feet below its lowest point.

Rook went first, because he was light, and the cable took his weight like a bowstring and sang a low, dead note. He moved quick and all angles, his coat of clinking pockets swinging, his copper hair bright in the grey light, and Elara watched him and thought: he carries other people's memories in those pockets, the shells of them, and the weight of them is what will kill him one day.

Halfway across, the cable gave a sound like a snapped harp string, and a strand under Rook's hand parted.

She saw it happen in pieces, the way you see a fall happening and cannot stop it: the strand letting go, Rook's weight swinging sideways, his hand closing on nothing, the coat's weight — all those clinking pockets, all that hoarded ghost — dragging him over the edge of the world. He did not scream. He went over the cable with his mouth open, and one hand caught a torn strand and held, and then he was hanging over the drop, the strand unraveling under his fingers, the cloud-sea spinning far below like a white mouth.

"Rook!" Elara was already moving down the cable.

But Devren was closer, and a soldier's body knows a fall before the mind does. He threw himself down the dead cable on his belly, the way he had thrown himself across rooftops a hundred times, reached the mooring collar, went over it without slowing — one hand on the sagging line, the other outstretched —

And caught Rook's wrist.

The two of them swung together over the drop, Devren's weight nearly pulling him off the cable, Rook's weight nearly pulling them both down, and for a long, terrible moment it was a balance, a hanging scale, the cable screaming against the collar. Devren's free hand was cut — a strand of broken braid had laid his palm open — and the blood ran down his wrist and over Rook's, hot in the cold air, and he did not let go.

"Stop kicking," he said, and his voice was very calm, the voice of a man who had pulled men out of the basin water a dozen times. "Stop fighting the wind. I've got you."

Rook stopped kicking. He hung there, breathing hard, looking up at the farm boy who had been ordered to end him three days ago, whose hand was bleeding over his, and something in his face broke open and mended in the same breath. Devren hauled. The cable dipped and sang, and then Rook's other hand came up, and his knee found the line, and he was back on the cable, shaking, the two of them lying on the swaying strand with their hands locked and both of them bleeding into the same small space between their palms.

Blood was shared. That was what it was — not an oath, not a ceremony, but blood running from one man's torn hand into another man's torn hand, and neither of them letting go.

"Your coat nearly killed you," Devren said, when he could speak.

Rook laughed — a short, broken sound, more sob than laugh. "My coat's carried me ten years." He looked at Devren's bleeding hand, at his own raw palms. "It's yours now, too. The weight of it."

Then Elara was there, kneeling on the cable, her bound arm moving stiffly as she reached down. She unwound her own linen binding — the one the scrounger matriarch had tied at dawn, the one that held the wound from the siphon — and tore it into two lengths, and wrapped one around Devren's cut palm and one around Rook's hands, tying them tight with the practiced knots of a girl who had bound her own wounds all her life.

"Your arm—" Rook started.

"It's healing," Elara said. "It's the least of us now." She finished the knot and sat back on her heels on the swaying cable, and looked at the two of them, and then at Sable, who had come down the line behind her, and she understood, in the way you understand a thing you have known all along, that they were not four people anymore.

They were a crew.

Sable knelt and looked at the binding, at the blood already soaking through, and her flat craftswoman's eyes went over the knots and found them sound. "Good work," she said. "Both of you." She looked at Devren. "That was a soldier's catch."

"It was a man's catch," Devren said. "The soldier part's on a fence post."

Rook looked at him, and the old measuring look — the hand inside the coat, the pricing of a stranger — was gone from his face, and something else was there in its place, something that had been waiting ten years to be given to someone. "Then it's a good catch, whatever it was," he said. "I owe you a song."

"You owe me a song," Devren said, and he was almost smiling, and for a moment the four of them sat on the cable high above the world and laughed, the sound thin and bright in the vast air, and below them the cloud-sea turned, and above them the belly of Aethon waited.

---

The anchorage at the end of the climb was a platform of rusted iron bolted to the under-hull, where the cables were moored by collars as wide as rooms. The four came up over the last mooring one at a time, stood on solid ground for the first time in hours, and looked up.

The city's belly filled the world above them — hull-plating the color of old bone, studded with hatches and ladder-shafts and the black mouths of service tunnels, all humming with the fat, fed hum of the Dreamfield coils, the same hum that had run through the Undertow's walls all her life, only here a thousand times stronger, a heartbeat under her feet, a hunger sleeping in the walls of the rich city.

Elara felt it reach for her.

Not awake — not the way the winch gate had woken. This was the deep, dreaming hunger of the whole lattice, vast and slow, tasting the air of its own belly and finding, faint as smoke, a signature it almost knew. She went still, and the ten thousand sank into their wards, and her mother's breath burned warm and small, and the hunger passed over her and did not wake.

It would wake, if they stayed. It would learn her, the way it had learned her in the freight yard. They had hours, maybe, before the upper city's coils tasted her properly — hours, and a whole city's worth of service tunnels to hide in.

Sable had the archive's maps spread on the iron, her finger tracing the lines of the underbelly — service tunnels, coil-lines, wind-posts, the spine of the Temenium rising through the clouds above them. "We're inside," she said. "The machine never watches the place where nobody survives the climb, and we survived it. That's worth something."

"We sang," Rook said quietly, flexing his bound hands. "That's what carried us. The song and the catch."

"The song and the catch," Sable repeated, and nodded, and rolled the maps away.

Elara stood at the edge of the platform with her hands on the cold rail and looked down, once, at the world she had come from — the grey fields, the basin, the far-off rooftops of the Undertow where Sila hummed her forgotten song and Nessa stared with open eyes and the scrounger matriarch sat by her fire waiting for the water to forget a girl who had already left it. Then she looked up, into the humming dark of the city that had eaten them, and the ten thousand stood in their wards behind her eyes, and Orrin's song was still in her throat, and her mother's breath was warm in the smallest room of her.

"We go up," she had said, at the foot of the trellis sea.

And now they were here.

Aethon slept above them on its stolen lives, vast and dreaming, and did not know — not yet — that four people had climbed into its belly carrying a city that wanted everything back. The coils hummed their one patient note, and the wind sang through the dead cables below them like a string being played, and Elara Voss, who had been nothing for sixteen years, stood at the threshold of the machine that had made her nothing, and was not afraid.

She was not empty. She had never been empty.

She was a city with a foundation, a crew at her back, a song in her throat, and a hand held out in the dark from three hundred years ago — and she was going to give them all back.

set.name: Elara Voss
set.description: Sixteen-year-old girl, born blank, carrying the forbidden archive—the life-memories of ten thousand erased people. CURRENT LOCATION: rusted anchorage platform on Aethon's under-hull at the summit of the trellis sea climb, at the threshold of the hull hatches and service tunnels, with Devren, Rook, and Sable; the climb is done and they have reached the belly of the rich city, whose Dreamfield coils sleep above in a vast hungry hum. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: exhausted but transformed; her left arm is no longer bound—she unwound her own linen binding (the scrounger matriarch's) and tore it into lengths to bandage Devren's cut palm and Rook's raw hands, so the siphon wound now rides unbound and healing; she crossed the one live (copper-fed) cable alone by deliberately emptying herself to NULL and felt the strange grief of becoming nothing on purpose; at the anchorage Aethon's deep lattice sensed a faint signature 'it almost knew' and passed over her, and she believes they have hours before it learns her properly. KNOWLEDGE: the full hidden history, the lattice by acceptance, the archive's maps/songs/blueprints, her mother's breath as anchor/address; the climber's ascent memory now named—a pre-Forgetting rope-walker called Orrin whose hands, rope-walking rhythm, and heartbeat song carried the crew up; the rule that the coils can only taste what they fed—dead mooring cables with no copper in the weave cannot taste her while fed cables with copper hum and would, so coil-fed ground must be crossed empty; Sable's underbelly maps (service tunnels, coil-lines, wind-posts, the Temenium's spine). RELATIONSHIPS: Sable Vey (teacher, rope-dance rear), Rook (keeper of his mother, promised return; she bound his hands), Devren (the deserting Enforcer now her crew—they sang together and she bound his cut palm), Orrin (the dead rigger whose memory and song are a hand held out in the dark), the ten thousand lives as wards with doors, Corvin Ash's charge. POSSESSIONS: patched trousers, rubberized vest (hem torn), catch-bag of stripped copper, arm wound unbound, Orrin's song in her throat. GOAL/STATE OF MIND: infiltrate Aethon's underbelly through the service tunnels before the deep coils wake and learn her signature, keep the ten thousand, Rook's mother, and Sila's song safe, live to give them all back; she has gathered a teacher, a trader, and a soldier, shared blood with them on the climb, and they are a crew.

set.name: Rook
set.description: Wiry ghost trader of the underlevels beneath the Undertow, copper-colored hair, coat of many clinking pockets, quick and all angles, eyes that price everything and rest nowhere. Stripped of his childhood (ages six through ten) by the high-tithe; spent ten years listening for his mother's voice in the residue trade. CURRENT LOCATION: anchorage platform on Aethon's under-hull at the summit of the trellis sea climb, with Elara, Sable, and Devren, at the threshold of the service tunnels into the rich city. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: shaken and raw-handed—on a thin dead cable a strand parted under him and the weight of his clinking coat dragged him over the edge of the world; Devren caught his wrist one-handed, was cut across the palm by broken braid, and hauled him back; Elara tore up her own arm-binding to wrap both their hands; his palms are now bound in her linen. He sang the rigger's song with the crew on the climb, then laughed and wept on the cable after the catch. The old measuring look he kept for Devren is gone—he stopped pricing the distance to the soldier's throat and knows the man is crew, and owes him a song. KNOWLEDGE: trader's lore, the hidden history, the certainty that his mother's memory is held whole in Elara's wards, the basin routes, Devren's dead-ground knowledge, and now the dead-cable/dead-residue rule of what the coils cannot taste. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (guide, ally, keeper of his mother), Sable (old contact, fully trusted), Devren (caught him over the drop, bled with him—'It's yours now, too. The weight of it'). GOAL: get the crew into Aethon's underbelly before the sweep finds them, keep Elara alive, hold the bright hope that his mother's laugh and lullaby are not lost.

set.name: Sable Vey
set.description: Disillusioned former memory-smith, one of the last who could calibrate Council extraction machines—she calibrated the machines that ate the Undertow's memories, including Rook's childhood, and walked off the floor after listening to a mother whose child the machine had taken. Grey hair cut short and uneven with a knife, fine-boned sharp face, hollowed craftswoman's eyes, flat voice. CURRENT LOCATION: anchorage platform on Aethon's under-hull at the summit of the trellis sea climb, with the crew, at the threshold of the upper city's service tunnels; satchel loaded with the archive's map-rolls, a handsaw, and a coil of wire. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: calm, terrible, and at brief moments almost warm—she led the rope dance from the rear, sang Orrin's rigger song with the crew, judged each dead cable with her craftswoman's eye ('The machine never learned them'), and on the anchorage spread the archive's underbelly maps across the iron and traced the way in: 'We're inside. The machine never watches the place where nobody survives the climb.' She accepts Devren now as crew, not merely a tactical asset, after his catch of Rook ('That was a soldier's catch'—'It was a man's catch'). She checked Elara's bindings and found them sound. KNOWLEDGE: everything from the hidden history, the lattice, the archive's maps/songs/blueprints, the dead-cable/dead-residue rule, and now the underbelly route into Aethon from the anchorage. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (the living vault who is a city with a foundation, the cause worth her guilt), Rook (old contact, fully trusted), Devren (a man now, blood shared with the crew). GOAL: get the crew inside Aethon's underbelly and into hiding before the deep coils wake, plan from the archive's blueprints, and atone for a lifetime of calibrating the machines that ate the world.

set.name: Devren
set.description: DESERTED Enforcer of the grey-green, now part of the crew; a farm boy from the Fringe who signed up to keep his family's land tax paid; a good soldier who dreamed of a world where his father's knife could be passed to his own child without irony, and who chose that world in a freight yard at dawn. CURRENT LOCATION: anchorage platform on Aethon's under-hull at the summit of the trellis sea climb, with Elara, Rook, and Sable, at the threshold of the service tunnels into the rich city. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: hollowed but newly certain; during the climb he caught Rook one-handed when the strand parted and the coat's weight dragged him over the drop—his free hand was cut open on broken braid, he held on and hauled the trader back with calm soldier's voice, and his palm is now bound in Elara's linen; they bled into the same small space between their hands. On reaching the anchorage he looked down through a gap in the cloud-sea at the sergeant's squad still walking its reader line and said a quiet 'Goodbye' to the coats he had worn. The knife, older than the Great Forgetting, remains warm against his ankle; his gloves are gone, his cut hand bound. KNOWLEDGE: patrol patterns and gate schedules of the freight district, rope-haul basin, and Fringe roads; every dead place where the coils cannot taste; the old rigger station at the trellis anchorage that garrison maps call a dead end; the dead-cable/dead-residue rule; the old Fringe way of listening with his feet. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (chose her in the freight yard, sang with her on the climb, stands beside her as crew), Sable (read him like a machine, now calls his catch sound), Rook (caught him over the drop, bled with him; Rook owes him a song and now calls him crew), Vane (former squad leader), his dead father and grandmother whose knife and listening-way guide him. GOAL/STATE OF MIND: infiltrate Aethon's underbelly with the crew, use his soldier's knowledge to keep them ahead of the manhunt his desertion triggered, and put himself fully on the side of remembering so he can one day pass the knife to his own child without shame. He is no longer on the side of forgetting.

The crew climbed the trellis sea—the cable web binding the Undertow to Aethon's belly—from the anchorage at the foot of the Fringe road. Elara used the pre-Forgetting rope-walker Orrin's archived memory (his hands, his walking rhythm, his heartbeat song) to guide them, keeping to dead mooring cables with no copper in their weave that the coils never fed and therefore cannot taste. On the one live copper-fed cable Elara crossed alone, deliberately emptying herself to NULL so the lattice tasted only a nothing. On a thin dead cable a strand parted under Rook and the weight of his clinking coat dragged him over the drop; Devren threw himself flat, caught his wrist one-handed (his own palm cut open on broken braid), and hauled him back. Elara tore up her arm binding and bandaged both their hands. The crew reached the anchorage platform on Aethon's under-hull; Aethon's deep coils sensed a faint signature 'it almost knew' through them but did not wake. The four are now a crew—blood shared, song shared, trust given.

Elara accessed and shared the archived memory of Orrin, a pre-Forgetting rigger who walked the trellis cables three hundred years ago and sang a heartbeat-rhythm song to keep his heart steady on the rope. All four crew members sang it ('When the world below is a far green sound...') during the climb, and Elara still carries it as a steadying song. The song is a located, accessible ward that can recur as a motif.

On the climb, Elara and Sable worked out the rule of what the coil lattice can and cannot taste: the coils only know what they fed. Dead mooring cables with no copper in their weave carry no lattice and cannot taste her, while live copper-fed cables hum and would learn her signature instantly. This dead-ground principle—move where the machine never drank—mirrors Devren's dead-residue routes on the ground and will govern the crew's movement inside Aethon's Dreamfield service tunnels.

To cross the one live copper-fed cable, Elara deliberately emptied herself—letting the ten thousand sink into their wards until only the smallest room holding her mother's breath remained—and crossed as a NULL, the machine tasting nothing. She felt a strange grief at becoming nothing on purpose but held her mother's breath as anchor. This is the first time she has chosen her blankness as a tool rather than endured it.

When Rook nearly fell from the thin dead cable and Devren caught his wrist one-handed, Devren's palm was laid open by broken braid; both men bled into the same small space between their hands and neither let go. Elara tore up her scrounger-matriarch arm binding to bandage them both; Rook told Devren the weight of his coat—and his hope—is now shared. The group became a crew on the anchorage: 'the song and the catch.'

Devren's right palm was cut open on broken braid during Rook's rescue and is now bound in Elara's linen (she tore up her own binding to wrap both their hands; her siphon wound now rides unbound). His bandaged hand must be worked around in the coming infiltration and later chapters so the injury and its shared-blood origin with Rook read consistently.

Rook's hands are raw and bound in Elara's linen after the fall; his coat's weight in many clinking pockets nearly killed him on the cable. The coat and the guilt-weight it carries ('It's yours now, too. The weight of it') should recur, and the bond of the shared blood with Devren should deepen as the crew operates inside Aethon.

Orrin the three-hundred-year-old rigger's heartbeat song ('When the world below is a far green sound...') now rides in Elara's throat and was sung by all four on the climb. It may recur as a steadying motif—particularly if the crew must again cross height or vertigo, or when Elara needs a grounding song inside Aethon's underbelly.

At the anchorage on Aethon's under-hull, the deep coils of the upper city sensed a faint signature they 'almost knew' in Elara and passed over her without waking. Elara judges they have hours before the upper lattice learns her properly. This must drive the urgency of the infiltration in Chapter 16 (Aethon's Underbelly), where Sable must keep to dead ground or mask Elara so the rich city's Dreamfield infrastructure does not trip alarms.

High on the trellis sea, Devren looked down through a gap in the cloud-sea and watched the sergeant's squad still walking its reader line across the Fringe fields; he said a quiet 'Goodbye' to the coats he had worn. The manhunt set off by his desertion and the winch-bridge cut continues below as the crew moves into Aethon—the net will likely keep searching the basin and Fringe while the crew is inside the city, narrowing their window to return.

chapters.name: Aethon's Underbelly
chapters.content:
The service hatch gave under Sable's hands with a sound like a sleeping animal turning over, and the crew stepped through the skin of the world into the dark.

It was warm inside. That was the first thing Elara noticed — warm the way a body is warm under a blanket, a close, breathing heat that smelled of hot copper and old oil and something sweet she could not name. The tunnel ran low, its ceiling strung with pipes and conduits and the coiled gut of the Dreamfield lattice, and every surface hummed — a fat, fed hum, the same one that had run through the walls of the Undertow all her life, but here it was not a whisper in the walls. Here it was the bloodstream. Here the machine did not lurk in the plaster; it was the bone and the marrow, the reason the floor was warm under her torn boots.

Sable moved first, sure-footed as a machine herself, the satchel of map-rolls across her back, her grey head tilted to read the pipes the way a sailor reads stars. "The old surveyor drew these tunnels as a body," she said, low. "Coil-lines are the veins. The wind-posts are the lungs. The Temenium's spine is the brain, and it's above us, all the way up through the clouds." She paused at a junction, ran her fingers over a valve the size of her head, and nodded to herself. "We're in the gut. If the machine ever notices us, it'll notice us the way it notices a swallowed bone."

"Then we'd best not be a bone," Rook said, and he was smiling in the dark, his bound hands flexing, and Elara saw that the trader who had priced every stranger for ten years had stopped pricing this city. He was looking at it the way he had looked at his mother's laugh — like a thing that could be carried home.

They followed the surveyor's body upward.

The underbelly was not one thing but a hundred things layered like the inside of a wound. They passed through a gallery of winch-rooms where cables the thickness of a man's waist ran into distant collars, wound and unwound by machines that never slept. They crossed a catwalk over a bay of holding tanks, and through a grate in the floor Elara saw, far below, the tops of clouds sliding past like a slow white sea, and the vertigo caught at her stomach until Orrin's song rose in her throat, and she hummed it, and her feet found their rhythm again.

Then they came to the first window into the city that had eaten them.

It was a glass pane set in a service door, meant for an engineer to check a pressure gauge, and through it Elara saw the rich city for the first time in her life. She had imagined it a thousand times from her vent above the Undertow — imagined marble and gold, towers that pierced the clouds. She had not imagined this. The corridor beyond the glass ran three storeys high, floored in pale stone that glowed faintly, and the people who walked it wore cloth that moved like water. A woman passed with a child on her hip, and the child laughed at something, and the woman laughed too, and Elara watched the laughter and knew, with a coldness that had nothing to do with the air, that not a moment of it was their own. They had bought it. Somewhere below, a mother's joy had been pulled out of her by a machine Sable had once calibrated, and bottled, and sold, and this woman wore it like a scarf.

"Don't watch," Sable said quietly. "You'll want to break the glass, and we can't afford the noise."

Elara watched one second longer. The child's laugh — bright, uncomplicated, the exact sound of a morning that had never been poisoned — came up through the pane and lodged in her chest like a splinter. Somewhere in her wards a door opened, and she felt the echo of it: a father's laugh in a wheat-field, a sister's shriek in a flooded street, ten thousand small bright sounds the machine had turned into currency.

"Who are they buying from?" she asked.

"Everyone," Sable said. "That's the machine's genius. It doesn't take from the desperate and sell to the rich — it takes from everyone and sells to everyone. The rich buy the poor's childhoods to feel young. The middling buy the rich's confidence to feel rich. A noble who's never held a plow buys a farmer's hands for a dinner party, then forgets he ever wore them by morning." Her flat voice did not change. "It's not theft. It's the economy. Theft would be a crime. This is a market."

Rook's face had gone still. "And a trader's job is to know the market," he said. "Ten years I moved those bottles. Ten years I carried other people's mothers in my pockets and called it trade." He looked down at his bound hands. "My coat's heavy," he said, and Elara heard, under the joke, the real weight of it.

"Your coat's going to be lighter," she said. "We're going to empty it."

He looked at her, and something in his face eased, and he nodded. "The song and the catch."

"The song and the catch," Devren repeated, and he was looking through the glass too, at the guards in grey-green at the far end of the glowing corridor, at the way the rich walked past them without seeing them, and his hand went, without permission, to his boot where the knife lay warm. "I wore those coats," he said. "Four years. I kept the peace so a woman could buy a child's laugh and forget it by dinner." He took his hand off the knife. "I'm going to make them remember."

---

Beyond the gallery the surveyor's body led them into the Dreamfield infrastructure itself, and there the city's true face showed itself.

The coil-chamber was a cavern. Lattice-stacks rose from the floor to the distant ceiling in rows like a forest of glass trees, each trunk a column of woven copper and crystal, each humming its particular note, and between the trunks ran channels of a pale, milky light — the same light Elara had seen in the memory barge's hold on the morning she had watched it ascend. Memory, running through the city like water through a heart. Workers in grey smocks moved between the stacks with brass readers on their belts, and Sable watched them with the flat, terrible stillness of a woman watching her own hands.

"I calibrated this," she said, very low. "Twenty years. I made the machines that made this light." She held up her hand and looked at it as if it belonged to someone else. "Every bottle in this city has my signature on it. I signed for them like a clerk signing for post."

Rook opened his mouth, reaching for the trader's easy comfort, but Devren got there first, and it was Devren's voice, flat and certain, that came out of the dark. "You signed for them," he said, "and then you walked off the floor. The machine's still here. You're not." He did not look at her. "There's a word for that where I come from. It's not 'clerk.'"

Sable was silent for a long moment. Then she said, "What's the word?"

"I don't know it yet," Devren said. "We're still writing it."

The crew moved on, and Elara found herself trailing behind, because the archive was stirring — not pressing, not drowning, but rising like the surface of a pool when something heavy has been dropped into it. The ten thousand knew this place. This cavern, this light, these stacks — this was where they had been sorted. She felt them reaching for the milky channels, felt the pull of a hundred thousand hands wanting what had been taken from them, and for a moment the wards buckled, and a man's voice came up through her, a deep voice full of a field at evening, and she heard him say his own name —

— Vess. My name is Vess. I had a daughter —

— and then her mother's breath burned warm in the smallest room of her, and the lattice steadied, and she let the voice flow through and back down into its ward, and she did not drown.

She stopped walking. "Sable."

Sable turned.

"They're awake in here," Elara said. "The ten thousand. This is where they were taken apart. Being here is like standing in the room where it happened to them." She pressed a hand to her chest. "They won't hurt me. But they want to come out. They want to be given back, and they can feel we're close to the place where they were put in."

Sable studied her, the craftswoman's eyes going over her face like a machine reading a calibration. "Then we hold them," she said. "You hold them, the way you held your mother. Not locked — held. Like a breath you're saving to sing." She came close and took Elara's face in both hands, the way the scrounger matriarch had, and for a moment her flat voice had something warm in it. "You're not going to break, Elara. You're the first vault the machine never got to fill. You were built to hold all of it and give it all back."

"Built," Elara repeated. "By him. By Valerius."

"Yes." Sable let her go. "And the machine never watches the thing it made and forgot. That's our only advantage, and it's a good one. We use it."

They moved on through the coil-chamber's far wall, into a service stair that spiraled up through the dark, and the hum grew and changed as they climbed, resolving out of the single note into a chord — and then into something like a voice. The stairs ended at a grate, and beyond the grate, through slats of iron, the crew saw the Temenium's spine.

It rose through the clouds like a cathedral's throat, a shaft of pale crystal and black iron the width of a street, and up it ran the light — not the milky light of the coils below, but a brighter, hungrier light, climbing toward the summit where the Temenium sat in its crown of weather. The city's memory, all of it, every stolen childhood and borrowed laugh and bottled mother, flowing up the spine into the machine that had eaten the world. The spine hummed in a chord so vast it was almost silent, and Elara felt the ten thousand lean toward it like iron filings toward a magnet, and she anchored on her mother's breath and held.

"All of it," Devren said, low, looking up. "Everything we ever were, going up that thing."

"Going up," Sable corrected, "and coming back down as power. Light. Heat. Manufactured souls." She nodded at the spine. "The rich don't buy memories because they're sentimental. They buy them because a stolen life is fuel. Every laugh that woman bought keeps a room warm for a week. Every childhood keeps a spire lit." Her voice was flat again, the flatness of a woman stating the exact dimensions of her guilt. "The machine doesn't steal to decorate. It steals to burn."

Elara looked up the spine, at the light climbing into the clouds, and felt the shape of it inside her — the blueprints, the surveyor's drawings, the feeding throat Sable had described in the bone-yard. She could see the whole city now as a single machine, a body with the Undertow for a root and the Temenium for a brain and every stolen life for blood, and she understood, with a clarity that frightened her, that it was not a monster that had grown by accident. It was a system. It had been designed. And it could be un-designed.

"Where do we hide?" Rook asked, and his voice was the trader's again, practical, pricing the next move. "The spine's watched. The coils are watched. We need a hole the machine doesn't think of as a hole."

Sable was already consulting the maps, her finger tracing the surveyor's lines. "The old maintenance crypt," she said. "Beneath the Temenium's base, where the builders lived while they raised the spine. Three hundred years old. The Council sealed it when the construction crews were retired. The maps call it a dead room. The machine never watches the place where nobody survives, and nobody survives the crypt." She looked up at them, and something almost like a smile crossed her face. "We've made a habit of those."

---

The crypt was exactly what the surveyor's memory promised: a vaulted chamber under the Temenium's foundation, reached through a rusted door behind a collapsed stair, the air dry and old and full of the ghost of builder's sweat. Coils of rusted cable lined the walls, and the floor was scattered with the tools of the men and women who had raised the spine three hundred years ago — a chisel, a leather glove gone stiff, a child's wooden wheel carved with a face that time had worn smooth.

And there, at the heart of the crypt, bolted to a table of iron, sat a machine.

Elara knew it before Sable said anything. The blueprint was in her like a second skeleton: the crown of coils, the chair with the leather straps, the feeding throat. It was an extraction machine — old, decommissioned, its crystal dark, its copper green with age — but it was an extraction machine, the same kind Sable had calibrated for twenty years, the same kind that had eaten Nessa's childhood and Rook's and ten thousand lives besides.

Sable stood over it in silence for a long time. Then she put her hand on the crown of coils, gently, the way you touch a sleeping animal you once loved and once feared.

"The first one they built," she said at last. "The prototype. They kept it down here to study, and then they forgot it, the way they forgot the builders." She turned to Elara, and her eyes were bright and terrible. "You asked me, in the bone-yard, how we give ten thousand people back when their owners are gone. I didn't know the answer then. I think I'm starting to see it." She touched the machine's dark crystal. "Everything that takes can be taught to give."

Elara looked at the machine, and then at the spine humming above them through the ceiling, and then at her crew — Devren with his hand on the knife that remembered, Rook with his bound hands and his coat full of ghosts, Sable with her guilt and her terrible hope — and she felt the ten thousand settle in their wards, patient now, waiting, the way water waits for the thaw.

"We need a plan," she said. "We've seen what the machine does with what it takes. We're inside it now, in the place it doesn't watch, with the blueprints in my head and the hands that built it on this table." She looked up, and her voice was quiet and certain. "Sable. You said the Temenium has one throat. One place where everything it has eaten flows through on the way to becoming power."

"Yes."

"Then we don't attack the city," Elara said. "We don't break the coils, we don't burn the spires. We go to the throat. And we teach the machine to give back."

The crypt was silent around them, full of the hum of the living city above, and the four of them stood in the dead room beneath the brain of the world and looked at each other, and the plan that would become their war was born there, in the dark, among the tools of the builders who had raised the spine and been forgotten for it.

"Tomorrow," Sable said. "We learn the throat's schedule. We learn the guards' pattern. We learn everything the machine knows about itself, and then we use it."

"And tonight?" Rook asked.

Sable looked at the extraction machine, at its dark crystal and green copper, and for the first time in twenty years, she smiled. It was a terrible smile, full of reckoning. "Tonight," she said, "we teach the prototype to give back."

Far above them, through a hundred feet of iron and crystal, the Temenium ate the world's memories and made them into light, and did not know — not yet — that four people had climbed into its belly carrying a city that wanted everything back, and that one of them had been built, three hundred years ago, to hold it all and let it go.

Elara Voss lay down in the crypt on a bed of builder's sacks, her mother's breath warm in the smallest room of her, the ten thousand waiting in their wards like a held breath, and slept the sleep of someone who had finally come home to the machine that had made her, and was no longer afraid of it.

The coils hummed their one patient note above her.

She dreamed of the throat of the world, and of teaching it to sing.

set.name: Elara Voss
set.description: Sixteen-year-old girl, born blank, carrying the forbidden archive—the life-memories of ten thousand erased people. CURRENT LOCATION: hidden with the crew in the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium's base in Aethon's underbelly, reached via the service tunnels and Dreamfield coil infrastructure; she slept there on a bed of builder's sacks and dreamed of the Temenium's throat. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: exhausted but transformed and newly unafraid; her left arm's siphon wound rides unbound and healing; she crossed the rich city's underbelly keeping herself small and anchored; inside the coil-chamber the ten thousand stirred violently (a farmer named Vess with a daughter surfaced and nearly buckled the wards) and she steadied them by anchoring on her mother's breath—'held like a breath you're saving to sing'; Sable took her face in both hands and told her she is the first vault the machine never got to fill, built to hold all of it and give it all back. KNOWLEDGE: the full hidden history; the lattice by acceptance; the archive's maps/songs/blueprints; her mother's breath as anchor/address; Orrin's rigger song ('When the world below is a far green sound...'); the coils-fed rule (dead cables/cables the machine never drank cannot taste her); Sable's underbelly routes; now the lived geography of Aethon's underbelly—winch galleries, holding-tank bays, the Dreamfield coil-chamber where memory runs in milky channels, the Temenium's spine rising through the clouds as the single feeding throat of the whole system; the prototype extraction machine bolted to an iron table in the crypt, which Sable means to teach to give; her own growing conviction, voiced to the crew in the crypt, that the plan is not to break the coils or burn the spires but to go to the throat and teach the machine to give back. RELATIONSHIPS: Sable Vey (teacher, guide, now her steadier—'You're not going to break, Elara'), Rook (keeper of his mother, promised return; lighter in the underbelly, calls the mission emptying his coat), Devren (the deserting Enforcer, crew, sang with her, bound his cut palm), Orrin (dead rigger whose song steadies her on heights), the ten thousand as wards who wake and reach toward the coil-chamber where they were sorted, Corvin Ash's charge. POSSESSIONS: patched trousers, rubberized vest (hem torn), catch-bag of stripped copper, arm wound unbound, Orrin's song in her throat. GOAL/STATE OF MIND: learn the Temenium's throat schedule and guard patterns from the crypt, teach the prototype to give back, keep the ten thousand and Rook's mother and Sila's song safe, and eventually teach the great machine to return everything; she has seen what extracted memories become (power, luxury, manufactured souls) and is no longer afraid of the machine that made her.

set.name: Rook
set.description: Wiry ghost trader of the underlevels beneath the Undertow, copper-colored hair, coat of many clinking pockets, quick and all angles, eyes that price everything and rest nowhere—though inside Aethon he has stopped pricing the city and started looking at it 'the way he looked at his mother's laugh—like a thing that could be carried home.' Stripped of his childhood (ages six through ten); spent ten years listening for his mother's voice in the residue trade. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium with the crew; he helped carry them through the service tunnels and the Dreamfield coil-chamber. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: hands still raw and bound in Elara's linen after the trellis fall; shaken into hope by what he saw in the underbelly—ten years carrying other people's mothers in his pockets and calling it trade ('My coat's heavy'—now answered by Elara's promise that they will empty it); the old measuring look for Devren is gone and he called out 'The song and the catch' as their creed. KNOWLEDGE: trader's lore, the hidden history, the certainty his mother's memory is held whole in Elara's wards, the basin routes, Devren's dead-ground knowledge, the coils-fed rule, and now the underbelly's geography and the truth that the memory trade he worked in was the machine's economy ('It's not theft. It's the economy.'). RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (guide, ally, keeper of his mother, now his promise of a lighter coat), Sable (old contact, fully trusted), Devren (caught him over the drop, bled with him, now crew and owed a song). GOAL: help the crew plan from the crypt, survive inside Aethon, keep Elara alive, and hold the hope that his mother's laugh and lullaby are not lost.

set.name: Sable Vey
set.description: Disillusioned former memory-smith, one of the last who could calibrate Council extraction machines—she calibrated the machines that ate the Undertow's memories, including Rook's childhood, and walked off the floor after listening to a mother whose child the machine had taken. Grey hair cut short and uneven with a knife, fine-boned sharp face, hollowed craftswoman's eyes, flat voice. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium's base with the crew, after navigating them through Aethon's service tunnels and Dreamfield coil infrastructure by the surveyor's maps ('the coil-lines are the veins, the wind-posts the lungs, the Temenium's spine the brain'). PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: calm, terrible, and at moments almost warm; in the coil-chamber she watched her own work with the flat stillness of a woman watching her own hands ('Every bottle in this city has my signature on it'), and Devren answered her confession by telling her she walked off the floor and there is a word for that they are still writing; in the crypt she found the prototype extraction machine and smiled for the first time in twenty years—'a terrible smile, full of reckoning.' KNOWLEDGE: everything from the hidden history, the lattice, the archive's maps/songs/blueprints, the dead-cable/dead-residue rules, the underbelly routes, the Temenium's single feeding throat, and now the prototype machine and her realization that 'everything that takes can be taught to give'; she resolved to spend the night teaching the prototype to give back, and to learn the throat's schedule and guard patterns tomorrow. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (the living vault who is a city with a foundation, the cause worth her guilt—she took Elara's face in her hands and steadied her in the coil-chamber), Rook (old contact, fully trusted), Devren (a man now, crew, who named her better than a clerk). GOAL: plan the strike on the Temenium's throat from the crypt, teach the prototype to give back, and atone for a lifetime of calibrating the machines that ate the world.

set.name: Devren
set.description: DESERTED Enforcer of the grey-green, now part of the crew; a farm boy from the Fringe who signed up to keep his family's land tax paid; a good soldier who dreamed of a world where his father's knife could be passed to his own child without irony, and who chose that world in a freight yard at dawn. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium with the crew. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: hollowed but newly certain; his cut right palm remains bound in Elara's linen (the shared-blood catch of Rook); inside Aethon he saw guards in grey-green walking the rich corridors and his hand went without permission to the knife in his boot before he took it away—'I kept the peace so a woman could buy a child's laugh and forget it by dinner. I'm going to make them remember'; he answered Sable's confession in the coil-chamber ('You signed for them, and then you walked off the floor... There's a word for that where I come from. It's not clerk.') and told her they are still writing it. KNOWLEDGE: patrol patterns and gate schedules of the freight district, rope-haul basin, and Fringe roads; every dead place where the coils cannot taste; the coils-fed rule; the old Fringe way of listening with his feet; and now the underbelly's geography and the truth of what the memory trade is for. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (chose her in the freight yard, stands beside her as crew, follows her new plan to the throat), Sable (crew, told her she is more than a clerk), Rook (caught him over the drop, bled with him, owed a song), Vane (former squad leader), his dead father and grandmother whose knife and listening-way guide him. GOAL/STATE OF MIND: keep the crew ahead of the manhunt his desertion triggered, plan the strike on the Temenium's throat from the crypt, and put himself fully on the side of remembering so he can one day pass the knife to his own child without shame.

The crew passed through the service hatch from the anchorage into Aethon's underbelly: winch-rooms with waist-thick cables, a catwalk over holding tanks above the cloud-sea, and a glass pane in a service door where Elara saw the rich city for the first time—a woman with a child on her hip laughing, the laugh itself bought and worn like a scarf. Sable explained the machine's economy: it does not steal to decorate, it steals to burn; a stolen life is fuel (a bought laugh keeps a room warm for a week, a childhood keeps a spire lit); 'it's not theft, it's the economy.' Rook confronted his ten years moving memory-bottles ('I carried other people's mothers in my pockets and called it trade'), and Elara promised they will empty his coat.

In the Dreamfield coil-chamber—where memory runs in milky channels between lattice-stacks and workers in grey smocks tend the stacks—the ten thousand inside Elara stirred violently, reaching for the light of the place where they had been sorted and taken apart; a farmer's voice (Vess, who had a daughter) surfaced and nearly buckled her wards. Elara steadied them by anchoring on her mother's breath, letting the voice flow through and back down, and Sable steadied her by taking her face in both hands: 'You're the first vault the machine never got to fill. You were built to hold all of it and give it all back.' The archive's location-sensitivity to the Temenium's machinery is now established.

In the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium's base, the crew found the prototype extraction machine—the first one the Council built, with its crown of coils, strapped chair, feeding throat, dark crystal and green copper—bolted to an iron table among the tools of the builders who raised the spine three hundred years ago and were forgotten. Sable touched it 'the way you touch a sleeping animal you once loved and once feared,' realized that 'everything that takes can be taught to give,' smiled for the first time in twenty years, and resolved to teach the prototype to give back. Elara stated the crew's plan aloud: not to break the coils or burn the spires, but to go to the Temenium's single feeding throat and teach the machine to give back.

Elara slept in the crypt on builder's sacks, anchored on her mother's breath, and dreamed of the throat of the world and of teaching it to sing. This seeds the coming plan (Chapters 19-20) and the eventual reversal of the Temenium (Chapter 34).

In the crypt beneath the Temenium, Elara voiced the crew's strategy: not to break the coils or burn the spires, but to go to the Temenium's single feeding throat—the one place everything the machine has eaten flows through on the way to becoming power—and teach the machine to give back. Sable resolved to learn the throat's schedule and the guards' patterns tomorrow, and to teach the prototype extraction machine to give back tonight. This must build into Sable's sabotage plan in Chapter 19 (The Plan, built on the archive's blueprints) and the reversal of the Temenium in Chapter 34.

Sable found the prototype extraction machine in the crypt and, smiling for the first time in twenty years, said 'Tonight, we teach the prototype to give back.' The prototype—old, decommissioned, its crystal dark—remains bolted to the iron table in the crypt; whatever Sable learns from reversing it should inform the crew's later understanding of how to change the Temenium's fundamental instruction from take to return (Chapters 19, 34).

The forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium's base—where the builders lived while they raised the spine, sealed by the Council when the construction crews were retired, called a dead room on the maps—is now the crew's hideout inside Aethon. It must serve as their base for planning (Chapter 19) and for staging the infiltration of the coil chamber (Chapter 20).

The Enforcer manhunt set off by Devren's desertion and the winch-bridge cut continues below Aethon in the basin and Fringe—the sergeant's squad still walking its reader line—while the crew is inside the city. The window to return narrows as the hunt keeps searching the ground routes; this tension should inform the crew's exit from Aethon in Chapters 21-22 (Discovery, Across the Fringe), when they are driven out of the city into the Fringe.

chapters.name: The Remembrance Salon
chapters.content:
The crypt gave them up at dusk.

Sable woke them with her hand already on the door, the surveyor's maps rolled tight in her fist. "The throat feeds at the ninth hour," she said. "The guards change at the eighth. Between the change and the feed there's a window the size of a held breath, and we're going to breathe it." She looked at each of them in turn. "But we're not going to the throat tonight. We're going to see where the feed goes."

"Where it goes?" Devren asked. "You said it goes up. Power. Light."

"Most of it," Sable said. "Not all of it. Some of it the machine can't burn — too fine, too specific. The Temenium sorts that out and sells it where the burning won't waste it." Her mouth made a shape that was not a smile. "There's a room above us, three hundred years old, where the rich gather to drink what the machine saves. They call it the Remembrance Salon. I used to calibrate its feed-lines."

Elara understood, with a cold turn in her stomach, what Sable was proposing. "You want us to go in."

"I want you to see it," Sable said. "Once. So that when you teach the throat to give back, you know what it is you're giving to. The map of a thing is not the thing." She pulled on a grey smock from a builders' rack — the same grey the coil-workers wore — and held out three more. "We're service staff now. The rich don't see service staff. We are the room's furniture that moves."

Rook took a smock and held it up to the lamplight, his trader's eye running over the seams. "And the readers?"

"The Salon is a dead room," Sable said. "It was built before the coils fed the city, and the lattice was never run into its walls. The rich come here to forget the machine exists — they can't have the hum reminding them where the tears come from." She shrugged. "No coils, no readers that work, no taste of Elara. It's the safest place in Aethon for us, which is exactly why it's the worst."

---

The service passages to the Salon were a different animal than the coil-chambers. Here the walls were paneled, the pipes gilded, the floor under their feet soft with carpet that swallowed their footsteps. Elara kept herself small and NULL behind Sable's grey back, her patched trousers and torn vest hidden under the smock, her bare arm — the siphon wound, still healing, still unbound — tucked against her side like a secret.

Through a service door marked with a chipped enamel plate, Sable held up a hand, and they stopped.

The Remembrance Salon opened before them like a throat swallowing them whole.

It was a theater. Not the pit-theaters of the Undertow, where families packed onto benches to watch a lantern-shadows show, but a theater of the old kind: curved tiers of velvet boxes rising in a horseshoe around a stage, lit not by flame but by the pale, milky light of memory running in channels through the walls. The light moved. It flowed upward along the paneling like sap, and Elara watched it and knew it for what it was — the feed, the sorted surplus of the machine's harvest, delivered warm to the room where the rich came to drink it.

The boxes were full. Elara saw silk and linen and jewels that caught the moving light, faces smooth with bought youth, throats lifted to the stage. A woman in the nearest box wore a smile that did not reach her eyes, and Elara realized with a jolt that the smile itself was not hers — it was a shade, a cheaper kind of purchase, worn the way a poor girl wears a cast-off coat.

On the stage, a man in a grey robe stood beside a stand of crystal vials, each vial glowing with its own particular color. He spoke in a voice trained to sound like water.

"Tonight," the man said, "we have something rare. A harvest from the deep holdings — a Fringe farm, three days east. A father's love for his dying daughter." He held up a vial of pale gold. "Seven years of it. Every morning he carried her to the window to see the light. Every night he sang her the same song. He did not know she could not hear him at the end. He sang anyway." The man's voice softened, a craftsman's softness. "This is not fuel. This is not warmth. This is a heart, still beating. And tonight, it is for sale."

There was a murmur in the boxes, a rustle of interest like wind through leaves.

"Seven years of a farmer's love," the man repeated. "Bought and worn. Felt entirely, and then, by morning, gone." He smiled. "The machine remembers. You need not. That is the contract we offer: all the feeling, none of the cost."

Rook made a sound low in his throat, and Devren's hand closed over his arm, a grip that said wait.

In the box nearest the stage, a noble rose. She was old in the way the rich were old — a face kept smooth by other people's years, hair kept dark by other people's childhoods — and her hands trembled as she raised a number. The bidding went quickly. The farmer's love was a fine vintage, and the room knew it. In the end the old woman won it, and the grey man came up the stairs himself, the vial in both hands like a chalice, and placed it in hers.

The old woman held the vial to the light. Then she uncorked it and drank.

---

The change came over her like weather.

Elara watched from the service door, one hand pressed to her chest where the ten thousand stirred — not violently, not in the coil-chamber way, but with a grief so old it had no edges. Somewhere in the deep wards a door opened, and she felt him: the farmer, the man named Vess, standing at a window with a child light as a bird in his arms, singing a song she could almost hear.

On the stage, the old woman's face broke open.

She did not sob like a rich woman. She sobbed like a father. It came up out of her in a sound Elara had heard once, in the weaver's block, the night Nessa was returned to Onna with nothing behind her eyes — a sound with no shape left in it, a sound the body makes when the heart has been asked to carry more than a heart can hold. The old woman fell to her knees in her velvet box, her hands clutching the arms of the chair, and she wept for a daughter who was not hers, a girl she had never met, a girl dying of a sickness that had never touched her.

"I can't," the old woman gasped, to no one. "I can't let her go. I can't — she's so small — she doesn't understand —"

Around her, the other nobles watched with polite, practiced stillness, the way you watch weather through glass. Some dabbed at their own eyes, moved by her, moved by the old woman's grief, moved by the grief they were allowed to share without owning.

Elara watched the farmer's love pour through a stranger's face and understood, in the same instant, two things at once.

The first was the obscenity. She had known it, of course — she had watched a Council taster drink a weaver's mother like wine from the memory barge, she had watched a rich woman wear a child's laugh like a scarf through a service-door pane. But knowing and seeing were different. Seeing was this: a man's whole heart, seven years of it, the exact shape of a father's devotion, poured into a woman who would forget it by dinner. The machine did not steal memories. It stole the having. It took the one thing the farmer had that the machine could not burn — the thing that was too fine to be fuel — and sold it to a woman who could not keep it, and called the whole transaction mercy.

And the second thing she understood was this: you could not fix a thing like this. You could not patch it. You could not regulate it, or tax it, or reform it, because the taking was not a flaw in the machine. The taking was the machine. The room she stood in, the velvet and the moving light and the weeping noble and the singing farmer in her wards — all of it was the same single act, performed over and over for three hundred years: reach in, take what is not yours, and call it living richly.

The Council could be stopped. Elara knew that now — she had known it since the freight yard, since the trellis sea, since she had stood in the crypt and named the throat as their target. Stopping was easy. You could stop a machine with a crowbar, a charge, a broken coil.

But this room could not be stopped. It could only be unmade.

She said it aloud, very low, to herself. "It can't be stopped. It has to be unmade."

Sable heard her. Sable, standing at her shoulder in her grey smock, watching the old woman weep with the flat, terrible stillness of a woman who had calibrated the machine that made this room possible. "Yes," she said. "That's what you came to see."

---

The evening wore on. The old woman's sobs ran their course and softened into hiccups, and then into silence, and then — Elara watched it happen, watched the exact moment the seven years of a farmer's love slid off her like water off a roof — into forgetfulness. The noble rose from her knees, dabbed at her eyes with a handkerchief her own mother's hands had never held, and smiled a placid, satisfied smile. She rang a small bell, and a servant came, and she ordered wine, and she did not remember a single thing.

By evening, as the Salon's milky light began to dim toward the feed's next hour, she was laughing at a joke in the next box, light and easy, her bought face smooth, her bought years bright.

Elara watched her and felt the ten thousand move in their wards like a sea turning. Not drowning. Waiting. The farmer's voice — Vess, my name is Vess — sang its daughter's song somewhere deep in her, and she held it, the way she had held her mother's breath, the way she would hold all of it until the day she opened her hands.

"Come," Sable said quietly. "We've seen enough. We have a window to breathe and a throat to learn."

They went back the way they had come, down the gilded service passages into the dark of the underbelly, and the hum of the machine rose around them again like a returning tide. Rook walked beside Elara, and his face was the face of a man who had spent ten years moving bottles and had just seen what was in them.

"My coat," he said at last, "is not heavy enough. It's not heavy enough by half. I want to know whose hands carried that girl to the window. I want to know her name."

"The machine knows," Elara said. "It's in the feed, in the sorted surplus, in the records of the Salon. Sable can find it."

"Then we find it," Rook said. "And when the throat gives back, that love goes home. All of it. Seven years, door to door."

Elara looked at him — at the trader who had priced the world for ten years and had finally stopped pricing it — and she nodded. "Door to door," she said.

They reached the rusted door of the crypt, and Sable barred it behind them, and the four of them stood in the dead room beneath the brain of the world with the evening's seeing still raw in them.

"Tomorrow," Sable said, "we learn the throat. The schedule. The guards. The one window the size of a held breath." She looked at the prototype extraction machine on its iron table, its dark crystal patient in the lamplight. "And we keep teaching this one to give back, until the teaching takes."

Devren drew his father's knife and laid it on the table, and the old blade lay there catching the light, remembering things the machine never got to eat. "Whatever we do," he said, "we do it to that room. To the Salon. To the boxes and the vials and the bells. We unmake the whole of it, or we unmake nothing."

"Then we unmake the whole of it," Elara said, and her voice was quiet and certain in the dark, and the ten thousand turned in their wards like a held breath waiting to be sung, and far above them the Temenium ate the world's hearts and made them into light, and did not know — not yet — that in its own dead room, a girl built to hold everything had finally seen the shape of the thing she was going to unmake.

She lay down on the builder's sacks, her mother's breath warm in the smallest room of her, and slept, and dreamed of a father carrying his daughter to a window, and of teaching the throat of the world to sing it home.

set.name: Elara Voss
set.description: Sixteen-year-old girl, born blank, carrying the forbidden archive—the life-memories of ten thousand erased people. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium's base in Aethon's underbelly, just returned with the crew from infiltrating the Remembrance Salon disguised in a coil-worker's grey smock (over her patched trousers and torn vest, left arm's healing siphon wound still unbound, tucked against her side). PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: exhausted but transformed and newly unafraid; the Salon visit changed her—she watched a noblewoman drink seven years of a Fringe farmer's love for his dying daughter, sob like a father, and forget it by evening, and she understood with full clarity that the taking is not a flaw in the machine but the machine itself: the Council cannot merely be stopped, it must be unmade. In the Salon, Vess (the farmer from the coil-chamber) surfaced with his daughter-song and now rests as a located ward; she held him the way she held her mother's breath. She slept on the builder's sacks afterward, dreaming of a father carrying his daughter to a window and of teaching the throat of the world to sing it home. KNOWLEDGE: everything prior (hidden history, lattice by acceptance, maps/songs/blueprints, mother's breath as anchor, coils-fed rule, underbelly geography, the throat plan, prototype machine), plus the lived shape of the Remembrance Salon—a three-hundred-year-old dead room built before the coils, its walls never run with lattice, so no readers work there and she is untasted in it; the Salon sells the machine's sorted surplus, the memories too fine to burn as fuel (love, specific grief) as consumables to the rich; Sable once calibrated its feed-lines. RELATIONSHIPS: Sable (teacher, steadier, now complicit witness of her own work), Rook (keeper of his mother; they sealed the promise that the farmer's love goes home door to door), Devren (crew; his knife on the table, his vow to unmake the whole system), the ten thousand as wards (Vess's daughter-song newly located), Corvin Ash's charge. POSSESSIONS: patched trousers, rubberized vest (hem torn), catch-bag of stripped copper, grey coil-worker's smock (disguise), Orrin's song in her throat. GOAL/STATE OF MIND: learn the throat's schedule and guard patterns, keep teaching the prototype to give back, then go to the single feeding throat and teach the great machine to return everything—and now, having seen the Salon, unmake the whole architecture of taking, not merely stop it.

set.name: Rook
set.description: Wiry ghost trader of the underlevels, copper-colored hair, coat of many clinking pockets, eyes that priced everything for ten years and now rest. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium with the crew, just returned from the Remembrance Salon in a grey service smock. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: hands still raw and bound in Elara's linen; shaken to the bone by what he saw in the Salon—ten years he moved bottles, and now he has seen what is in them: 'My coat's not heavy enough. It's not heavy enough by half.' He wants to know the name of the farmer's dying daughter, whose love was sold and forgotten, and he swore the seven years will go home 'door to door' when the throat gives back; Elara agreed. The measuring look for Devren is long gone; the crew creed stands: 'the song and the catch.' KNOWLEDGE: trader's lore, the hidden history, the located honey-lit kitchen lullaby of his mother, the coils-fed rule, the underbelly's geography, and now the Remembrance Salon's economy—the sorted surplus too fine to burn sold as consumable hearts. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (keeper of his mother, now keeper of the farmer's love he means to send home), Sable (fully trusted), Devren (crew, bled with him). GOAL: learn the Salon records to find the farmer's name and daughter's name, help plan the strike on the throat, survive inside Aethon, and empty his coat of every carried ghost—his mother's first, then all the rest, door to door.

set.name: Sable Vey
set.description: Disillusioned former memory-smith who calibrated Council extraction machines, including the machines that ate Rook's childhood and the Undertow's memories; grey hair cut short with a knife, fine-boned sharp face, hollowed craftswoman's eyes, flat voice. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium's base with the crew, just led them through the gilded service passages into the Remembrance Salon in a grey coil-worker's smock and back out through the Salon's one window of safety (a dead room with no lattice in its walls). PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: calm, terrible, and at moments almost warm; in the Salon she watched a noblewoman drink a farmer's love and forget it by evening with the flat, terrible stillness of a woman watching her own hands—she herself calibrated the Salon's feed-lines; her guilt now has a room attached to it. She reaffirmed tonight's work: keep teaching the prototype to give back until the teaching takes, and learn the throat's schedule and guards tomorrow. KNOWLEDGE: everything prior (hidden history, maps, dead-cable/dead-residue rules, underbelly routes, the throat, the prototype), plus the Salon's layout and feed schedule, its dead-room nature, and the ninth-hour feed/eighth-hour guard-change window she named for the crew. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (the living vault, the cause worth her guilt), Rook (old contact, fully trusted), Devren (crew; his knife and his vow on the table). GOAL: plan the strike on the Temenium's throat, unmake the whole architecture of taking including the Salon, and atone for a lifetime of calibrating the machine that sells hearts in velvet boxes.

set.name: Devren
set.description: DESERTED Enforcer of the grey-green, now crew; Fringe farm boy, good soldier who chose remembering in a freight yard at dawn. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium with the crew, just returned from the Remembrance Salon in a grey service smock. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: hollowed but newly certain; cut right palm bound in Elara's linen; in the Salon he watched the noblewoman's bought grief with the stillness of a man who once policed such rooms, and afterward drew his father's knife and laid it on the iron table, vowing: 'Whatever we do, we do it to that room—to the Salon, to the boxes and the vials and the bells. We unmake the whole of it, or we unmake nothing.' Elara agreed. KNOWLEDGE: patrol patterns and gate schedules, every dead place the coils cannot taste, the coils-fed rule, the Fringe way of listening with his feet, the underbelly's geography, and now the Salon's existence and its dead-room safety. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (chose her; follows her plan to the throat), Sable (crew), Rook (bled with him, owed a song), his dead father and grandmother, his father's knife that remembers things the machine never got to eat. GOAL: plan and carry the strike on the throat, unmake the whole system—the Salon and the boxes and the vials—so he can one day pass the knife to his own child without irony or shame.

At dusk Sable woke the crew and led them through gilded service passages into the Remembrance Salon, a three-hundred-year-old theater of velvet boxes and milky memory-light inside the Temenium's base, disguised as coil-workers in grey smocks from a builders' rack. The Salon is a dead room: it was built before the coils fed the city and the lattice was never run into its walls, so no readers work there and Elara is untasted in it—the safest place in Aethon for them, and therefore, as Sable said, the worst. It sells the machine's sorted surplus: the memories too fine or specific to burn as fuel (love, particular grief) sold as consumables to the rich. Sable once calibrated its feed-lines. The crew left through the same dead-room window, having seen where the feed goes.

In the Remembrance Salon, a noblewoman bought and drank seven years of a Fringe farmer's love for his dying daughter—'Vess, my name is Vess, I had a daughter'—the same farmer who surfaced in the coil-chamber. She sobbed like a father in her velvet box, clutching the chair, weeping for a child who was not hers, while the other nobles watched with polite stillness, and then by evening she forgot it entirely, laughing at a joke in the next box, her bought face smooth. Inside Elara, Vess's daughter-song surfaced and now rests as a located ward, held the way she holds her mother's breath.

Watching the noblewoman weep and then forget, Elara understood two things at once: the obscenity of the Salon—the machine does not steal memories, it steals the having, selling a father's whole heart to a woman who cannot keep it—and that the taking is not a flaw in the machine but the machine itself. She said aloud, low: 'It can't be stopped. It has to be unmade.' Sable confirmed: 'That's what you came to see.' This conviction—stop nothing, unmake the whole architecture of taking—now shapes the crew's war.

After the Salon, Rook said his coat 'is not heavy enough by half' and demanded to know whose hands carried the farmer's daughter to the window and her name, saying the machine's records in the Salon hold it. Elara promised they will find it. He swore the farmer's seven years of love will go home 'door to door' when the throat gives back, and Elara agreed: 'Door to door.'

Back in the crypt, Devren drew his father's knife and laid it on the iron table, declaring that whatever they do must be done to the Salon—'to the boxes and the vials and the bells. We unmake the whole of it, or we unmake nothing.' Elara agreed: 'Then we unmake the whole of it.' The crew's mission is now explicitly the unmaking of the system, not merely stopping the machine.

Vess's seven years of love for his dying daughter now rest in Elara as a located ward (his daughter-song, held like her mother's breath). Rook vowed the love goes home 'door to door' when the throat gives back, and Elara agreed; they mean to learn the farmer's name and the daughter's name from Salon records. This specific memory should be among those the Temenium returns to their owners in Chapter 35 (The Descent), and Vess himself may matter as the face of the system's cruelty.

The Remembrance Salon is a dead room inside the Temenium's base—built before the coils, no lattice in its walls, readers dead, Elara untasted—and Sable knows its layout, feed schedule (ninth-hour feed, eighth-hour guard change), and its service passages. This is a strategic resource inside Aethon that the crew could use again (hiding, staging, or as a place of reckoning), particularly during the infiltration and the fall of the city (Chapters 19-21, 29-35).

Elara's Salon-born conviction—the Council cannot merely be stopped, it must be unmade, because the taking is the machine itself—shapes the plan in Chapter 19 (The Plan), the strike on the throat in Chapter 20, and the fundamental reversal from take to return in Chapter 34 (The Temenium), and it underlies her refusal of Valerius's bargain in Chapter 32: she does not want a given past, she wants a future built by unmaking the architecture of taking.

chapters.name: The Face of Valerius
chapters.content:
The broadcast found them in the middle of the night, in the middle of the teaching, in the dead room beneath the brain of the world.

Sable had the prototype's crown open, its dark crystal lifted out and laid on the iron table like a heart removed from a chest, and she was drawing in the air above it with a brass stylus, tracing the paths of the old feed. The teaching had been going well. That was the terrible part of it, later — how well it had been going. For three nights she had fed the machine back its own language, reversing the polarity of the take, and that night, for the first time, a sliver of something had come out of the crystal instead of going in. A thread of light the color of a remembered summer, thin as spider-silk, rising off the dark stone and hanging in the dead air, and Sable's flat voice had cracked on the word "Look," and they had all leaned in like children at a window.

And then the wall behind the prototype had lit up like a wound.

Elara felt it first, because she always felt it first. The lattice — the deep lattice of the city, the Dreamfield roots that fed everything — woke all at once, not humming but screaming, and the scream ran through the crypt's dead walls the way water finds a crack, and every one of the ten thousand voices in her turned at once, the way a crowd turns when it hears its own name called out of the dark.

"Down," Sable said, but it was too late, and she knew it. The light was already coming.

It came through the ceiling and the walls like it owned them — which it did — a pale, hungry light that gathered in the center of the crypt and flattened into a sheet, and within the sheet a shape. Not a man, at first. A face the size of a doorway, assembled out of the light itself, and Elara looked at it and felt the floor drop out of her stomach, because she knew that face. She had never seen it before in her life. But it was made of ten thousand other faces, and she carried all of them.

The face of Valerius was a face the way a crowd is a face. Every feature was borrowed. The brow was a barge-worker's brow, three hundred years dead. The eyes were a mother's eyes, taken with her grief and her daughter and her last morning in a wheat-field. The mouth was a soldier's mouth, opened around a name he never got to finish saying. It was smooth and young and terrible, a composite of swallowed lifetimes, and beneath the surface of it Elara could feel the ten thousand shift and press against their wards like birds against a window, because some of them recognized the face that had eaten them.

"That's him," Rook breathed, and his bound hands were white at the knuckles. "That's the — that's him."

"It's not him," Sable said, but her voice was wrong, and they all heard it. "It's a broadcast. A projection. The machine's mouth." She was backing away from the prototype, her hands still open, as if she could shield the sliver of remembered summer from the light's attention. "It's a message. It doesn't know we're here."

The face opened its borrowed mouth, and the voice that came out of it was not one voice. It was a chord — ten thousand voices singing the same words at once, laid over each other so thickly that the shape of the sound was smooth. The voice spoke, and every coil in Aethon carried it, and every brass reader in every district repeated it, and far below, in the water-stained Undertow, in the weaver's block on Level Nine, in the dry vaulted nest of the scroungers and the dead sorting floors and the bone-yard, the words came into every room that had a wall.

"CITIZENS OF AETHON. CITIZENS OF THE DEEP DISTRICTS. I SPEAK TO YOU FROM THE TEMENIUM, WHOSE HEART IS YOURS, WHOSE MEMORY IS THE CITY."

The voice paused, and in the pause Elara heard, very far down, the sound of her own Undertow: the drip of water, the hum of a coil, a child crying in a room she would never see again. The broadcast reached everywhere. It had reached there. It was, right now, speaking over her mother's alcove.

"FOR THREE HUNDRED YEARS WE HAVE KEPT YOU. WE HAVE TAKEN THE BURDEN OF YOUR PASTS SO THAT YOU MIGHT LIVE CLEAN. THIS IS THE CONTRACT. THIS IS THE MERCY."

Devren's hand had gone to his boot without his permission, and his father's knife was out, the old blade catching the pale light, and he was standing in front of Elara, between her and the face, the way he had once stood between her and a squad of Enforcers in a freight yard at dawn. He was shaking. They could all see it. "He knows," Devren said. "He's talking about us. He's talking about —"

"Quiet," Sable said. "Listen."

"— AND YET THERE IS A SICKNESS IN THE MEMORY OF THE CITY. A CONTAMINATION. SOMETHING UNBORN AND UNTASTED HAS ENTERED THE LATTICE. IT WALKS IN THE DEEP PLACES. IT CARRIES WHAT WAS ERASED, AND IT MEANS TO GIVE IT BACK."

The face of Valerius smiled, and it was ten thousand smiles, and not one of them reached the borrowed eyes.

"THIS IS NOT THE WAY OF THE MERCY. THIS IS THE WAY OF THE FLOOD. MEMORY UNRETURNED IS PAIN. MEMORY RETURNED IS DROWNING. THOSE WHO WOULD DROWN THE CITY FOR THE SAKE OF THE DEAD ARE NOT SAVIORS. THEY ARE THE TIDE, AND THE TIDE MUST BE TURNED."

The light in the crypt had gone colder. The sliver of remembered summer had died on the table, its thread of color gone grey, and Sable stood over the open prototype with her hands at her sides and her face a mask of flatness that Elara had learned to read: it was the face Sable wore when the thing she had calibrated was doing exactly what she had taught it to do.

"THEREFORE, BY THE AUTHORITY OF THE MEMORIAN COUNCIL, I DECLARE A PURGE OF MEMORY CONTAMINATION. ALL DREAMFIELD COILS WILL BE RE-CALIBRATED TO THE PUREST NOTE. ALL READERS WILL BE TURNED TO A NEW SIGNATURE. EVERY LIFE IN THE CITY — ABOVE AND BELOW — WILL BE SWEPT FOR THE CONTAMINATION, AND EVERY SWEEP WILL BE PAID FOR IN THE COIN THE CITY KNOWS BEST."

The chord of voices paused again, and when it resumed, it was softer, almost gentle, the gentleness of a machine that had learned mercy from ten thousand mouths.

"THE TIDE WILL BE TURNED. THE ERASED WILL STAY ERASED. THE CLEAN WILL STAY CLEAN. AND THE CITY — THE CITY WILL REMEMBER NOTHING OF THIS MORNING, BECAUSE THE MORNING IS NOT OURS TO KEEP."

The face of Valerius dissolved into light, and the light into the ordinary dark of the crypt, and the hum of the coils returned, one note, patient, the way it had always hummed — as if nothing had happened, as if the brain of the world had not just opened its mouth over the whole sky.

For a long moment no one moved.

Then Rook said, very quietly, "It's a reader."

Sable turned her head. "What?"

"A reader," Rook repeated. "The ghost trade has a saying. You don't need to know what you're looking for to sweep for it — you just need to know the one thing it isn't. He's not hunting the archive. He's hunting the one signature in the whole city that reads NULL on every plate, the one life that was never harvested, the one —" He stopped, and looked at Elara, and the look was the look of a man who had just priced a thing and found it too dear to carry. "He's sweeping for a blank. He's sweeping for you."
