The crypt was silent. The prototype's open heart lay dark on the iron table. Far above, the Temenium hummed its one patient note.

"All of it," Devren said at last, and his voice was hoarse. "Every coil in the city, turned to one note. Every reader, turned to one signature. When he sweeps, he'll find her the way you find a hole in a net by running your hand over every thread." He looked down at the knife in his hand, and then at Elara, and the old blade caught the lamplight, remembering. "They're not coming down here to look for us. They're going to make the whole city into a reader and let it tell them where we are."

"No," Sable said, and they all turned to her. She was standing over the prototype, her hand on its dark crystal, and her flat voice had gone strange — not afraid, not angry, but the voice of a craftswoman doing arithmetic at the edge of a drop. "The whole city as a reader is a blunt instrument. You can't sweep a thousand rooms with one note. You have to give the note a home — you have to re-calibrate district by district, block by block, coil by coil, until every thread has felt the NULL and reported it. That's not a day's work. That's a season's work." She looked up, and her eyes were bright and terrible. "He's not going to sweep us out tomorrow. He's going to sweep us out the day after, and the day after that, and every day until the net closes. The purge is a net, and the net is tightening around the whole city, and we are standing in the middle of it."

"And the Salon?" Rook asked. "The dead room? The one place the coils never ran?"

"Dead," Sable said, and she said it like a door closing. "The purge re-calibrates everything. A dead room is only dead while the lattice forgets it exists. A purge is the lattice remembering every room it ever touched — and the Salon, for all its dead walls, is fed by the machine. The feed-lines I calibrated are still in its walls. When they turn the note to NULL-hunting, the Salon's own feed will tell them where the room is, and a room the machine feeds is a room the machine can taste."

Elara stood very still in the middle of the dead room, feeling the ten thousand in their wards, feeling the shape of the thing that had just happened to them, and understood that Sable was right. It was not a threat. It was a schedule. The purge did not mean the machine was afraid — it meant the machine had finally, after three hundred years, noticed the one thing it had made and forgotten, and it was going to spend a season of days hunting it down, block by block, coil by coil, until the NULL was a known quantity and the blank was a cleaned surface.

They were out of time. Not tomorrow — they had never had a tomorrow. They had a morning, maybe two, before the first re-calibrated coils reached the Temenium's base and tasted the crypt's dead walls and found the girl who carried ten thousand people.

Sable looked at the prototype, its heart still open on the table, the sliver of remembered summer dead and gone. "The teaching," she said, and her voice cracked on the word. "It was working. It was just starting to work. The first thread of give, in three hundred years. And now —"

"Now we don't have three more nights," Elara said, and her voice was quiet and certain, and the ten thousand turned in their wards to listen, because they knew that voice. It was the voice that had named the throat. "We don't have to teach the prototype to give back in a season. We have to teach the throat to give back before the net closes." She looked at Sable, at Devren, at Rook. "Sable. You said the purge re-calibrates coil by coil. District by district. How long until it reaches the Temenium's base?"

Sable was already doing the arithmetic, her craftswoman's hands moving in the air the way they moved over a machine. "The coils feed up from the districts. The Undertow first, then the Fringe lines, then the deep service web, then the base of the spine." She stopped, and the arithmetic settled into something flat and terrible. "Three days. If they're thorough. Two, if they cut corners."

"Two days," Elara said. "Then we go to the throat tonight — not tomorrow. Tonight, before the first re-calibrated coil learns the shape of the NULL." She looked at the prototype's open heart, at the dark crystal that had, for one sliver of a moment, given back a remembered summer. "We don't finish the teaching here. We take it to the machine itself. We teach the throat the way we were going to teach the prototype — except we do it in two days, with the whole city turned into a net closing around us, and the face of the man who built us watching from the top of the world."

The crypt was silent. The hum of the coils was one patient note, patient as a heartbeat, patient as a held breath.

Rook was the first to move. He reached into his coat and took out a bottle — one of his own, a trader's bottle, the kind he had moved for ten years — and he set it on the iron table beside the prototype's dark heart, and he looked at it for a long moment, and then he looked at Elara.

"Two days, then," he said. "I've got a coat full of ghosts and a debt to a farmer whose name I still don't know. We're going to need faster than two days to make that right, so we'd best make the two days count." He nodded at the bottle. "That's the last of the good residue. Strongest stuff I ever carried. If we're going to walk into the throat of the machine, we might want something that remembers harder than the world does, in case the world forgets us."

Devren sheathed his father's knife with a sound like a door shutting, and when he looked up, his face was the face of a man who had already chosen, who had chosen in a freight yard at dawn and was choosing again now, with the net closing and the face of the High Memorian still burning behind his eyes. "Two days," he said. "The Salon. The boxes. The vials. The bells. We unmake the whole of it, or we unmake nothing. And we start tonight."

Sable looked at the three of them, and then at the prototype, and she put her hand once more on its dark crystal — the way you touch a sleeping animal you once loved and once feared — and when she spoke, her flat voice was the voice of a woman who had finally, after twenty years of calibrating the take, found the one thing worth calibrating the give.

"Tonight," she said. "We learn the throat's guards. We learn the feed. We learn the one window the size of a held breath — and we breathe it." She looked up at the ceiling, at the place where the spine ran up through the clouds toward the crown of weather where the Temenium sat, and her mouth made the shape of a smile that was not a smile. "And we teach the machine that took the world to give it back. Before the tide turns on us."

Elara stood at the center of them, the ten thousand waiting in their wards like a held breath, her mother's breath warm in the smallest room of her, the face of Valerius still burning behind her eyes — a face made of swallowed lifetimes, a face made partly of people she carried, a face that had looked out over the whole city and promised to keep them erased.

She looked at the prototype's dark heart on the iron table, and at Rook's last bottle, and at Devren's sheathed knife, and at Sable's steady hands.

"Two days," she said. "We make them count."

And far above them, through a hundred feet of iron and crystal, the Temenium ate the world's memories and made them into light, and the first coils of the purge began their patient re-calibration, district by district, thread by thread — the whole city turning itself into a reader, a net, a single enormous hand reaching down through the dark toward the one girl built to hold everything, who had finally run out of time to learn to let it go.

They had two days. They had each other. They had the song and the catch.

They began.

set.name: Elara Voss
set.description: Sixteen-year-old girl, born blank, carrying the forbidden archive—the life-memories of ten thousand erased people. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium's base in Aethon's underbelly, mid-night after the Remembrance Salon; she and the crew just witnessed the High Memorian's broadcast in the crypt's own walls. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: newly hardened, out of time but unbroken; she watched the face of Valerius—a composite of swallowed lifetimes assembled from faces she carries—announce a city-wide purge of memory contamination sweeping for the NULL, for her; she felt the ten thousand turn in their wards at the broadcast, and understood in the same breath that the purge is a schedule, not a threat, and that they have roughly two days before the re-calibrated coils reach the Temenium's base and taste the crypt. She held the crew together, converting panic into a deadline: the throat is struck tonight, not tomorrow; they cannot finish teaching the prototype, so they will carry the teaching to the machine itself. KNOWLEDGE: everything prior (hidden history, lattice by acceptance, maps/songs/blueprints, mother's breath as anchor, coils-fed rule, underbelly geography, throat plan, Salon's dead-room and economy), plus the broadcast's content and its meaning: Valerius sensed the archive's presence and declared a purge; all coils will be re-calibrated to one 'purest note' hunting the NULL signature; all readers re-tuned; every sweep paid for in taken memory. She carries Vess's daughter-song as a located ward and Rook's mother's laugh, and knows Rook set his last bottle of residue on the table as their good-luck ghost. RELATIONSHIPS: Sable (who named the two-to-three-day arithmetic and the dead-room caveat about Salon feed-lines), Rook (who named the purge for what it is—a reader sweeping for the one signature that reads NULL), Devren (who drew his father's knife and stood between her and the face), the ten thousand as wards, Corvin Ash's charge. POSSESSIONS: patched trousers, rubberized vest (hem torn), catch-bag, grey coil-worker's smock, Orrin's song in her throat. GOAL/STATE OF MIND: strike the Temenium's throat within the two-day window—teach the great machine to give back before the purge net closes, unmake the whole architecture of taking (the Salon, the boxes, the vials, the bells) rather than merely stop it, and give everything back door to door.

set.name: Rook
set.description: Wiry ghost trader of the underlevels, copper-colored hair, coat of many clinking pockets, hands still bound in Elara's linen. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium with the crew, just after the Valerius broadcast. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: grim, sharp, and all the more resolute; he named the purge for what it is—not a hunt for the archive but a reader sweeping for the one signature in the whole city that reads NULL, for Elara—and said it with the trader's cold clarity. He set his last bottle of good residue on the iron table as their talisman: 'if we're going to walk into the throat of the machine, we might want something that remembers harder than the world does, in case the world forgets us.' He still burns with the promise to return the farmer's seven years of love door to door and to learn the daughter's name, and acknowledged the cruelty of the timing: 'I've got a coat full of ghosts and a debt to a farmer whose name I still don't know.' KNOWLEDGE: trader's lore, ghost-residue lore (the sweep-for-what-it-isn't saying), hidden history, his mother's located lullaby, coils-fed rule, underbelly geography, Salon economy, and now the purge's mechanics as he reads them. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (keeper of his mother and of the farmer's love), Sable, Devren (bled with him), his coat of ghosts. POSSESSIONS: clinking coat, last bottle of residue on the crypt table. GOAL: help strike the throat within two days, empty his coat of every carried ghost—his mother's first, then all the rest, door to door.

set.name: Sable Vey
set.description: Disillusioned former memory-smith who calibrated Council extraction machines for twenty years, grey hair cut short, flat voice. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium's base with the crew, the prototype's crown open and its dark crystal laid on the iron table, immediately after the Valerius broadcast. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: calm, terrible, cracked open at the edges; the teaching was working—for the first time in three hundred years a sliver of give, a thread of remembered summer, had risen off the prototype's crystal—when the broadcast killed the thread and she had to watch her own calibration turned to the purge. She named the purge's true shape: re-calibration district by district, coil by coil, a net that tightens day by day, roughly two to three days before it reaches the Temenium's base; and she delivered the death of their safe ground: the Salon's dead-room status is voided by its feed-lines, which she herself calibrated and which will let the purge taste the room. She resolved to compress the plan: strike the throat tonight, carry the teaching to the machine itself. KNOWLEDGE: everything prior plus the purge mechanics and the two-to-three-day arithmetic. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (the living vault, the cause), Rook, Devren, the prototype (sleeping animal once loved and once feared). GOAL: teach the throat to give back inside the two-day window, unmake the architecture of taking, atone.

set.name: Devren
set.description: DESERTED Enforcer of the grey-green, now crew; Fringe farm boy; right palm bound in Elara's linen. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium with the crew, after the Valerius broadcast. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: white-knuckled and newly certain; the moment the face of Valerius lit the crypt walls he drew his father's knife without permission and stood between Elara and the face, the way he once stood between her and his squad in a freight yard. He saw the purge for what it means on the ground—the whole city turned into a reader that will find Elara the way you find a hole in a net by running your hand over every thread—and answered the deadline with his vow unchanged: 'The Salon. The boxes. The vials. The bells. We unmake the whole of it, or we unmake nothing. And we start tonight.' He sheathed the knife with a sound like a door shutting. KNOWLEDGE: patrol patterns, gate schedules, coils-fed rule, dead places, underbelly geography, Salon, purge implications. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (chose her; stands between her and the machine), Sable, Rook, his father's knife that remembers. GOAL: carry the strike on the throat within two days so he can one day pass the knife to his own child without irony or shame.

In the dead-room crypt beneath the Temenium's base, in the middle of the night, while Sable was teaching the prototype to give back (its dark crystal open on the iron table, a sliver of remembered summer rising off it for the first time in three hundred years), the city's Dreamfield lattice woke screaming and the wall lit up with a broadcast: the face of Valerius, assembled out of the light itself—a composite of swallowed lifetimes, brow of a dead barge-worker, eyes of a mother taken with her daughter, mouth of a soldier opened around an unfinished name. His voice was a chord of ten thousand voices, heard through every coil and every brass reader in every district, down into the Undertow and the weaver's block. He declared a sickness in the memory of the city—'something unborn and untasted has entered the lattice... it carries what was erased, and it means to give it back'—and announced a PURGE OF MEMORY CONTAMINATION: all Dreamfield coils re-calibrated to the purest note, all readers turned to a new signature, every life in the city swept, every sweep paid for in taken memory, with the promise 'the erased will stay erased.' The sliver of give died on the table as he spoke. Rook named the purge for what it is: a reader sweeping for the one signature that reads NULL on every plate—a blank, Elara. The crew realized Valerius sensed the archive's presence. They are out of time.

Sable did the arithmetic aloud: the purge re-calibrates the coils district by district, block by block, coil by coil—Undertow first, then the Fringe lines, then the deep service web, then the base of the spine—roughly three days if thorough, two if corners are cut, before the net reaches the Temenium's base and tastes the crypt. She also delivered the death of the crew's safest ground: the Remembrance Salon's dead-room status is voided by the purge, because its feed-lines (which she herself calibrated) run in its walls and a room the machine feeds is a room the machine can taste. This compressed the crew's plan: strike the throat tonight, not tomorrow; carry the teaching to the machine itself within the two-day window.

After the broadcast, Rook took from his coat his last bottle of good ghost-trade residue—the strongest he ever carried—and set it on the iron table beside the prototype's dark heart, saying if they are going to walk into the throat of the machine they might want something that remembers harder than the world does, in case the world forgets them. The bottle remains on the crypt's iron table, a talisman and a resource.

Valerius's broadcast declared a city-wide purge of memory contamination: all Dreamfield coils re-calibrated to one purest note hunting the NULL signature, all readers re-tuned, every life swept. Sable's arithmetic gives the crew roughly two to three days before the re-calibrated coils reach the Temenium's base and taste the crypt (and the dead-room Salon via its feed-lines). This countdown must drive the plan in Chapter 19 (The Plan) and the infiltration in Chapter 20 (The Dreamfield Coils), where an Enforcer alarm trips and the crew has mere minutes instead of the hour they expected; it also shapes their discovery and flight in Chapter 21.

The broadcast proved Valerius sensed the archive's presence—he called it a contamination 'carrying what was erased' that 'means to give it back.' The High Memorian is now actively hunting the NULL, and the crew knows his face is a mask of swallowed lifetimes (a composite of the very people Elara carries). This knowledge must inform the confrontation with Valerius in Chapters 31-33 (The Wind-Posts, The Bargain, The Hollow Gaze at Last), where Elara faces the machine wearing a man's shape and refuses a fabricated past.

Sable determined that the Remembrance Salon's dead-room status is voided by the purge: its feed-lines (which she calibrated) run in its walls, and a room the machine feeds is a room the machine can taste once the coils are re-calibrated to hunt the NULL. The Salon can no longer be assumed safe as a hiding place or staging ground during the infiltration and fall of the city (Chapters 19-21, 29-35), though its service passages and records (including the farmer's name and his daughter's name, which Rook wants) remain a resource.

For the first time in three hundred years, the prototype extraction machine gave back: a thread of remembered summer rose off its dark crystal while Sable taught it, before the broadcast killed the sliver. The crew can no longer finish teaching the prototype in the crypt, so they will carry the teaching to the Temenium's throat itself—this seeds the counter-frequency work of Chapter 26 (The Song of the Discarded) and the fundamental reversal of the Temenium in Chapter 34 (from take to return).

chapters.name: The Plan
chapters.content:
The crypt was an island in the middle of the night. Above it the city hummed one patient note, but down in the builders' dead room the hum came muffled, a heartbeat heard through a wall, and the four of them sat around the iron table in the circle of a single lamp and laid the plan out like a hand of cards.

Sable went first, because it was her craft. She had unrolled the surveyor's drawings across the table, parchment crackling with three hundred years of dry air, and pinned the corners with Rook's last bottle of residue, Devren's sheathed knife, and a chisel left by a builder who had died before the spine was finished. The map showed Aethon from below, drawn as a body: the Dreamfield coil-lines running like veins through the districts, the feeding channels gathering in the service web, and the single throat where everything the city had eaten rose into the Temenium's spine.

"We can't break the coils," Sable said. "That was my first thought the night we came in. Cut the veins, starve the brain. But a machine that big doesn't die when you cut it — it cauterizes. The Council would seal the ruptured lines and re-route the feed, and we'd be a wound the city would spend a season healing, and the purge would find us in the scar tissue."

"Then we don't cut the veins," Devren said. "We agreed. The throat."

"The throat." Sable traced the line of the spine up through the clouds. "Everything the machine has eaten flows through one place on its way to becoming power. We can't reach its heart and we can't outrun its guards. But we don't have to. We only have to reach the coils at the base of the spine, where the feed gathers before it climbs."

Rook leaned in, bound hands flat on the table. "You said sabotage the coils and cripple the grid. Now you're saying the coils don't matter?"

"I'm saying the coils are the only part of the machine we can touch without being eaten." Sable's finger moved to the chamber they had crossed two nights ago. "The lattice-stacks are the machine's blood. They're what the purge is re-calibrating right now, district by district, to hunt the NULL. And a machine busy re-calibrating its blood to one note has to stop, for one moment, listening to anything else."

The silence around the table was the sound of a lock falling open.

"Two nights ago we stood in that chamber," Elara said slowly, "and the ten thousand rose in me like a tide. You said it yourself, Sable — this is where they were sorted. The lattice-stacks hold the shape of every life that ever fed them. They remember."

"They remember everything," Sable said. "That's the gift of the archive, and we're going to use it as a key. You, Elara, are going to feed the coils a memory-song."

"Feed the coils," Rook repeated. "You want her to sing to the machine?"

"Sing to it." Sable looked at Elara, and her craftswoman's eyes were bright and terrible. "The lattice is not a wall, it's a hunger. It drinks memory the way a root drinks water, and it cannot tell the difference between a memory given and a memory taken. That's the one door the machine never locked, because it never imagined anyone would walk through it from the inside. You carry ten thousand lives, and every one of them has a song. You give the coils a song to drink — a long, deep, old song — and while they lean into it, they won't feel the charges going in."

The word hung in the air: charges.

"How much do we need?" Devren's hand had gone to the knife on the table, not drawing it, just touching it.

"Not to destroy — Elara was right, we unmake, we don't burn. But to cripple, less than you'd think." Sable turned the map so they could all see the three points where the district channels met the base of the spine. "A charge at each of the three feed-nodes, timed to the heartbeat of the song. If they blow together, the coils seize — not dead, just stopped, long enough for the purge to stutter in its re-calibration and every reader in the city to go deaf for one hour."

"One hour," Rook said. "And in that hour?"

"In that hour we climb." Sable's finger moved to a small hatch the surveyor had drawn at the spine's base. "The builders' stair runs up the inside of the base, sealed when the construction crews were retired — same as this crypt. It opens into the throat chamber itself, and when the coils seize, the throat will be open and undefended, because every guard will be running to the blackout." She looked at Elara. "And then you teach the machine to give back. The way we taught the prototype, but faster, and all at once."

The crypt was very quiet. The lamp flame stood straight, and Rook's last bottle caught the light and held it, dark and patient.

"You said the teaching," Elara said. "The prototype only gave back a sliver after three nights, and that was just starting to work. How do we teach the whole machine in an hour?"

Sable was silent for a long moment. Then she turned the map so Elara could see it from her side. "The prototype is one machine. It learns slowly, the way you teach a horse to trust you. But the Temenium is the sum of every coil, every feed that ever touched a life. And you are not the prototype's crystal, Elara. You are ten thousand lives with the streets between them, and the machine that drank those lives still has their shape in its teeth." She tapped the point where the feeding channels joined the spine. "When you sing to the coils, you're not teaching a stranger. You're reminding a thief what it stole. It has held these songs for three hundred years. It knows them. All we're doing is giving the song back to the place that already remembers it — and asking it, for one hour, to give the rest back too."

Elara sat very still, feeling the ten thousand in their wards, feeling the shape of what Sable was asking. It was the same act she had done in the bone-yard and on the cable above the world: opening a door and letting a life flow through her without drowning. Only this time the life would flow out of her and into the machine, and the machine would drink it, and the drinking would change something.

She understood she was not going to be hidden this time. The coils were the purge's eyes, re-calibrated to hunt the NULL, to hunt her. And she was going to walk into the chamber and sing, and every coil in the city would taste her on purpose — and for the space of the song they would taste her as song, as life, as the thing they had always fed on, and the one signature they had been told to hunt would be indistinguishable from the meal they had always loved.

"It's a mask," she said. "Not a mask of NULL. A mask of everything."

"Yes," Sable said. "The one mask the machine cannot see through, because it's made of the machine's own food. The purge has turned the whole city into a net, and you cannot slip through a net by being nothing — not anymore. You slip through it by being everything at once."

"Before dawn," Devren said. It was not a question.

"Before dawn." Sable confirmed. "The first re-calibrated coils reach the Undertow by full light. If we wait for tomorrow, the net tightens past us. But the ninth-hour feed is the deep one — the one that pulls hardest from the districts — and it comes an hour before dawn. If we're in the chamber when it starts, the song will ride the feed itself. It will go up the spine and down into every district on the back of the city's own hunger, and when the charges blow, the whole grid will be singing our song for one hour whether it wants to or not."

"The ninth-hour feed," Rook repeated. "Sable, you said the Salon's feed was the ninth-hour feed. The one you calibrated."

"Yes." Sable's voice was very level. "Every feed-line I ever signed for comes together in that hour, in that chamber, at the base of the spine. Twenty years of my signature, all in one place, and I know exactly where the weakest joint of every one of them is." She looked at her own hands. "I spent twenty years learning how to take. There's no better education in how to give. Tonight I get to use it."

Devren had drawn his knife without meaning to, and he looked down at the old blade worn thin in the middle by three centuries of whetting. "And the guards? The chamber's watched — we saw it. Workers in grey smocks, brass readers on their belts."

"Workers in grey smocks who are paid in taken memory and forget their own names by the end of each shift." Sable looked at Elara. "We still have the builders' rack of smocks we took for the Salon. We wear them, and we walk in like we belong to the feed, because we do. And you, Elara — you don't sing loud enough for the workers to hear. You sing inside, the way you sang the lattice, and the coils will feel it the way they feel a memory being drunk, which is the only way they know how to feel anything."

Elara closed her eyes and reached into the wards. The songs were a tide beneath everything, and she let them rise until she could feel the shape of the one she needed: an old work-song, older than the Great Forgetting, sung by the builders while they raised the spine itself. It was a song about carrying — the weight on your back, the road under your feet, the singing that made the weight bearable — and it had been sung by men and women who would build the machine that would eat their grandchildren, and it had never once been sold.

She opened her mouth, and the song came out of her like water out of a cracked jar, not loud, but deep, one note under another, ten thousand voices folded into one. It rose through the crypt and into the walls, and for a moment even the dead room was alive with it, the dust trembling off the builders' tools, the lamp flame leaning toward her as if it too were thirsty.

She let it die away and opened her eyes.

"That's the song," Sable said, and her voice was hoarse. "The builders' own song. The machine remembers it — it fed on the builders, it's still feeding on their grandchildren — and it will lean into it like a hand it knows." She looked around the table. "We go at the change of the hour, when the night workers hand over to the feed shift. Three charges, three feed-nodes, set to the heartbeat of the song. Elara sings the coils under. Rook and I place the charges. Devren holds the door."

Devren looked up. "And if the door doesn't hold?"

"Then we're four people in the throat of the machine, and the machine wakes," Sable said, and the flatness of her voice was not calm, it was arithmetic. "But the purge gave us something, Devren. It told us when. The coils are re-calibrating district by district, and a machine that is re-calibrating is half-listening. We walk in while it's busy listening for the NULL, and we give it the one thing it never expected to hear: the sound of everything it already ate, coming home."

Rook took his last bottle off the map and held it up to the light, the way a man looks at a coin he is about to spend. "I've been pricing this moment for ten years. Every bottle I moved, I told myself the next one would be the one that led me home. And now we're walking into the machine that ate my mother's kitchen, and the plan is a song and a knife and a girl who can't be seen by anything except the thing we're about to feed." He set the bottle down in the center of the map, where the spine rose through the clouds. "I've made worse bets on better odds. I'm in."

Devren sheathed his knife with a sound like a door shutting. "I'm in."

Elara looked at the three of them, and at the map, and at the bottle standing at the heart of the machine like a single dark note, and she felt the ten thousand settle in their wards, patient, waiting, the way water waits for the thaw.

"Then we go before dawn." She looked at Sable. "Tell us the way in. The exact way. The one window the size of a held breath."

Sable put her finger on the small hatch at the base of the spine. "The builders' stair. It runs up the inside of the spine's base, behind the feed-gallery, sealed when they retired the construction crews — same as this crypt. Nobody's walked it in three hundred years. But the surveyor drew it, and you carry the surveyor." She looked at Elara. "You'll have to walk it first, by the map in your head, to open the far door from inside the gallery. Then we follow."

"And the chamber door itself?" Rook asked. "The one the workers use?"

"The feed-gallery has a service door on the north wall at the top of a ladder, under a vent the size of a man's hand. It's the door the calibration techs use at the change of shift, and it is never locked during the ninth hour, because the techs are paid to move fast and no one has ever thought to steal from the machine." Sable's mouth made the shape of a smile that was not a smile. "That's the window. The one thing the machine never locks is the door its own people walk through. We're its own people tonight. We wear its smocks, we carry its rhythm, we sing its song, and we walk through the door it left open for us."

The plan was done. It lay on the table under the lamp, pinned by a bottle and a knife and a builder's chisel, and it was impossible, and it was all they had.

Elara looked up at the ceiling, at the place where the spine ran up through the clouds toward the crown of weather where the Temenium sat and the face of Valerius waited, made of swallowed lifetimes, made partly of people she carried.

"One hour," she said. "One hour of the whole city deaf, and then the throat is ours. We teach it to give back, or we give ourselves teaching it." She stood, and the ten thousand rose with her, a tide inside her, patient and certain. "We go at the change of the hour. Rook, the bottle comes with us — if the machine forgets us, we want something that remembers harder than the world does." She looked at Sable. "You taught the prototype to give. Now you teach the throat."

"Now I teach the throat," Sable agreed, and for the first time since the broadcast, her flat voice had something like peace in it.

Devren stood and buckled his belt, his hand resting a moment on the knife at his boot, the knife that remembered. "Before dawn," he said, quiet.

"Before dawn," Elara said. "We make the count."

She reached for the map and began to fold it, and as she folded, the builders' old work-song rose again in her throat, and she let it out low and soft — not loud enough for the city, loud enough for the four of them, a promise carried in the only language the machine had ever spoken.

Carry the weight. Sing while you carry. The road knows your feet. The road is coming home.

The lamp burned. The bottle stood dark at the heart of the map. And above them, through a hundred feet of iron and crystal, the Temenium ate the world's memories and made them into light, and did not know — not yet — that before dawn, four people in its own grey smocks would walk through the door it never locked, carrying a song it had eaten three hundred years ago, and teach it, at last, to give the song back.

They had an hour. They had a song. They had each other.

They began to wait for the change of the hour, and the waiting was the hardest part, because in the waiting they could hear the purge moving through the city above them, district by district, coil by coil, the whole world turning itself into a net, and the net was coming down toward the place where they sat with a plan and a bottle and a knife that remembered, waiting for the door the machine had left open to swing wide and let them in.

set.name: Devren
set.description: DESERTED Enforcer of the grey-green, now crew; Fringe farm boy; right palm bound in Elara's linen. CURRENT LOCATION: the forgotten maintenance crypt beneath the Temenium with the crew, the hour before the ninth-hour feed; his father's knife lies on the table, and he has just taken the plan's hardest post. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: white-knuckled and newly certain; he drew his father's knife without meaning to while the plan was laid out, and answered the risk with the same arithmetic Sable used—if the door does not hold, they are four people in the throat of the machine and the machine wakes; he sheathed the knife with a sound like a door shutting and declared himself in. KNOWLEDGE: everything prior (patrol patterns, gate schedules, dead places, underbelly geography, Salon, purge implications) plus the plan: he holds the feed-gallery's north service door while Sable and Rook plant the charges and Elara sings; the crew moves at the change of shift wearing grey smocks; the seizure gives them one hour of deaf readers and an open throat. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (stands between her and the machine), Sable, Rook, his father's knife that remembers. GOAL: hold the door and carry the strike on the throat before dawn so he can one day pass the knife to his own child without irony or shame.

In the crypt beneath the Temenium in the hour before the ninth-hour feed, Sable laid out the plan on the surveyor's map pinned by Rook's last residue bottle, Devren's sheathed knife, and a builder's chisel: sabotage the Dreamfield coils, not by cutting the veins (the Council would cauterize and re-route) but with three charges at the three feed-nodes where the district channels meet the base of the spine, timed to the heartbeat of a memory-song; blown together, the coils seize—stopped, not dead—for one hour, every reader in the city deaf, the throat open and guards running to the blackout, during which the crew climbs the sealed builders' stair into the throat chamber itself. Entry is via the feed-gallery's north service door at the top of a ladder under a vent the size of a man's hand, never locked during the ninth-hour feed because no one has ever thought to steal from the machine; the crew will wear the grey smocks from the builders' rack and walk in as the machine's own people. The ninth-hour feed is the deep pull an hour before dawn, and the song will ride it up the spine and down into every district.

Sable's plan makes Elara the key: she will feed the coils a memory-song from inside the chamber—not loud enough for the workers to hear, sung inside the way she sang the lattice—and the coils, which cannot tell a memory given from a memory taken, will lean into it and not feel the charges going in. This is her mask against the purge: not NULL (which the re-calibrated net hunts) but everything at once, the machine's own food, the one mask the machine cannot see through because it is made of the machine's own meals.

Elara located and sang the builders' own work-song, older than the Great Forgetting, sung while the spine was raised—a song about carrying: the weight on your back, the road under your feet, the singing that makes the weight bearable. It was sung by the men and women who built the machine that would eat their grandchildren and was never once sold. The machine remembers it because it fed on the builders, and it will lean into the song like a hand it knows. The song is now a located, accessible ward in the archive and the plan's key.

The crew resolved to strike before dawn at the change of the hour, when the night workers hand over to the feed shift: Elara sings the coils under, Sable and Rook plant the three charges at the feed-nodes, Devren holds the door, and Rook's last residue bottle comes with them into the chamber as the thing that remembers harder than the world in case the machine forgets them. Sable: 'You taught the prototype to give. Now you teach the throat.' Elara: 'Before dawn. We make the count.' The plan is impossible and it is all they have; they sit in the crypt waiting for the change of the hour, hearing the purge moving toward them through the city.

The crew has resolved to strike before dawn at the change of the hour: infiltrate the feed-gallery in grey smocks through the north service door (never locked during the ninth-hour feed), Elara sings the builders' work-song to the coils as a mask of everything, Sable and Rook plant three charges at the three feed-nodes at the base of the spine timed to the song's heartbeat, Devren holds the door, and Rook carries his last residue bottle into the chamber. This plan must execute in Chapter 20 (The Dreamfield Coils), where an Enforcer alarm trips and the crew has mere minutes instead of the hour they expected.

If the three charges blow together at the feed-nodes, the coils seize—stopped, not dead—for one hour, deafening every reader in the city and opening the throat undefended while guards run to the blackout. The Chapter 20 infiltration depends on this seizure; its success or failure determines whether the crew reaches the throat chamber to teach the machine to give back (Chapters 20-21, and eventually Chapter 34).

The surveyor's map shows a sealed builders' stair running up the inside of the spine's base, opening into the throat chamber; Elara carries the surveyor and will have to walk it first, by the map in her head, to open the far door from inside the gallery. This is the crew's planned route into the throat chamber after the coils seize, and must carry into the infiltration and beyond.

The ninth-hour feed is the deep pull an hour before dawn; if Elara sings when it starts, the builders' song will ride the feed itself—up the spine and down into every district on the back of the city's own hunger—so that when the charges blow, the whole grid sings their song for one hour. This is the mechanism by which the strike shakes the whole city and by which the returned-memory motif begins; it should inform the discovery/flight (Chapter 21) and the eventual fall of Aethon (Chapters 29-35).

chapters.name: The Dreamfield Coils
chapters.content:
The change of the hour came up through the stone like a change in the weather.

In the crypt, the lamp had burned down to its last finger of wick, and the four of them stood in the circle of its failing light, shrugging into the grey coil-workers' smocks Sable had lifted from the builders' rack two nights ago. The cloth was stiff with three hundred years of dust and the ghost of sweat, and it smelled the way the crypt smelled — old, patient, and forgotten. Rook's coat went on over his smock, because the bottle was in its innermost pocket, and the bottle had to come with them, and he had said as much without being asked. Devren's knife went into the sheath sewn into his boot, under the grey hem, and he settled it the way other men settle a belt.

Sable went to the prototype for the last time. She stood over the machine whose crown of coils she had taught, for three nights, to give back a sliver of summer, and she touched its dark crystal the way you touch a sleeping animal you once loved and once feared.

"I'll come back for you," she said, so low only Elara heard it. "Or I won't. But the teaching goes on either way." She straightened, and her flat voice was level again. "We go. Elara first, up the builders' stair — you open the far door from inside. Then the rest of us through the feed-gallery's north door at the top of the ladder. Wait for the feed to start before you sing. Nothing is sung until the ninth hour."

Elara nodded. The builders' work-song waited in her throat like a held breath, older than the Great Forgetting, sung while the spine was raised, never once sold.

The stair was a wound in the stone behind the crypt's rusted door: a spiral so narrow she had to turn her shoulders, the steps worn to hollows by the feet of men and women who had climbed them three hundred years ago to raise the machine that would eat their grandchildren. She climbed by the surveyor's map in her head, counting the landings, feeling the air change — from the dry dead air of the crypt to the hot, fed, humming air of the living machine. The hum grew as she climbed, resolving out of a single note into a chord, and the chord into something that knew her.

At the top of the stair a door waited, sealed with the same rust that had sealed the crypt. She put her shoulder to it, and it gave with a shriek of old iron that she felt in her teeth, and she stepped out into the feed-gallery.

The gallery ran along the north wall of the Dreamfield coil-chamber, a narrow walkway of iron grating suspended a hundred feet above the chamber floor, screened from the stacks below by a fretwork of perforated panels. Through the holes Elara saw the machine the way Sable had taught her to see it: not a cavern but a body. Lattice-stacks rose in rows like a forest of glass trees, each trunk a column of woven copper and crystal, each humming its note; between the trunks ran the channels of milky light, memory moving through the city like water through a heart. The workers moved below in their grey smocks, small and quiet, tending the stacks with brass readers on their belts, paid in taken memory, forgetting their own names by the end of each shift.

And there, where the district channels met the base of the spine, Elara saw the three feed-nodes — the great collars where the milky rivers gathered before they climbed. They were the heart of the plan. Three charges, timed to the heartbeat of the song.

She found the north service door at the top of her ladder, exactly where the surveyor drew it, under a vent the size of a man's hand, and she unlatched it from the inside and left it ajar for the others, the way Sable had said — never locked during the ninth hour, because no one had ever thought to steal from the machine.

Then she found her place, at the rail of the gallery where the three feed-nodes stood in her line of sight, and she waited, with the ten thousand settled in their wards like water waiting for the thaw, and the builders' song in her throat like a seed.

The workers below changed. The night shift handed over to the feed shift, grey smocks passing grey smocks, brass readers changing belts, and the hum of the chamber dropped a note as the machine turned its attention to the deep pull — the ninth-hour feed, the one that pulled hardest from the districts, the one that came an hour before dawn.

A bell rang, far off, patient as a heartbeat.

The feed began.

Elara felt it before she heard it: the whole chamber leaning, the milky light in the channels quickening, the lattice-stacks drinking deeper, and the first faint cries of the Undertow rising up the feed-lines, a hundred thousand stolen mornings pulled up the spine to be burned. And she opened her mouth, and she sang.

Not loud. The workers below did not look up. She sang inside, the way she had sung the lattice in the bone-yard, and the song came out of her like water out of a cracked jar — the builders' work-song, the one about carrying, the weight on your back, the road under your feet, the singing that made the weight bearable. She let it flow out of her and down the gallery and into the stacks, and the machine, which could not tell a memory given from a memory taken, leaned into it like a hand it knew. It remembered this song. It had fed on the builders; it was still feeding on their grandchildren; and the song rose up out of the dark of its own memory and drank.

Behind her, quiet as ghosts in grey smocks, Sable and Rook came up the ladder through the north door and slipped down the gallery to the first feed-node. Devren took the door, closing it to a crack, and stood with his back to the wall where the ladder came up, his hand at his boot, watching the chamber below with the flat, patient stillness of a man who had guarded worse things.

The song rode the feed. Elara felt it go up the spine and down into every district on the back of the city's own hunger, felt it wash into the Undertow, into the weaver's block where Sila slept her hollow sleep, into the Fringe where the sergeant's squad still walked its reader line, and for one long, held moment the whole grid sang their song.

At the first feed-node, Sable's hands moved in the dark of her smock, setting the charge to the heartbeat of the song, her craftswoman's fingers finding the weakest joint of a feed-line she had signed for twenty years ago. At the second node, Rook worked beside her, his bound hands steady, the last bottle in his pocket like a second heart. Elara sang, and the song rose, and the machine drank.

The plan was nearly done. The third node waited at the far end of the gallery, in the shadow of the spine itself, and Sable was already moving toward it, her step sure as a machine, when Elara felt it — a wrongness in the hum, a note that did not belong. Not a new note. An old one. A familiar one.

She opened her eyes.

At the far end of the chamber, a door had opened at the base of the spine, and a man in the grey-green of the Enforcers stood in it, holding a brass reader the size of a child's head, and the reader was singing.

Not the NULL-quiet. Not the choked silence of a dead room. The reader was singing the builders' song — the exact song Elara was pouring into the stacks — and the man's face, lit by the milky light, was the face of a man who had been sent to listen for one signature and had found, instead, the sound of everything.

The Enforcer raised the reader higher, and the song in it sharpened, and Elara saw his mouth move — shouting — and the chamber answered.

The alarm was not a bell. It was the lattice itself, screaming. Every stack in the cavern rang out on one raw note, a note that tore through the hum like a blade through cloth, and the milky light in the channels flared white, and the workers below dropped their readers and ran. The feed did not stop — the machine was too vast to stop — but the chamber changed in an instant from a sleeping animal to a woken one, and everywhere at once, doors were sealing, lights were coming up, and the sound of boots was coming down the gallery stairs.

Sable's voice, flat even in the ruin of it: "They're on the purge watch. They've been listening for NULL and they heard everything instead. We have minutes. Not the hour."

"Minutes for what?" Rook's hand was already in his coat. "The charges are set — two of three. We blow what we have?"

Sable looked at the third node, forty feet away through the gap where the alarm had come in, where grey-green shapes were already spilling through the door at the base of the spine. "We blow what we have," she said, "or we don't blow at all. Two nodes, one live line — the seizure will be dirty. Half the city deaf instead of all of it. The throat stays locked."

Elara did not stop singing. She could not stop. The song was the mask, and the mask was everything — the only thing keeping the re-calibrated purge net from tasting her as the NULL it hunted, and if she stopped, the whole chamber would know in one breath exactly what she was. She sang, and the song shook with the alarm, and the ten thousand rose in her like a tide and steadied, and she felt the third node at the far end of the gallery, still bare of its charge, and she understood the count.

Devren was already moving. He came down the gallery toward the spine-side door with his father's knife drawn, the old blade worn thin in the middle by three centuries of whetting, and he put himself between the grey-green shapes and Sable's back, and his voice came out flat and certain: "Set the third one. I hold the door."

"Two men with readers," Sable said. "They'll taste her the second you move."

"Then I don't give them a second." Devren took one step forward, and the knife caught the milky light, and Elara sang, and the song went out of her like a river in flood, and she knew — with the clarity that came only in the seconds before a thing broke — that she had to stop hiding behind the song and become it.

She stopped singing with her mouth. She let the song go all the way out of her, past the mask, into the one thing the machine could not refuse. The builders' song poured through her and into the stacks, and the stacks poured it back, and the whole chamber sang, and the alarm note broke against it and went silent, and for one instant — one full, held, impossible instant — the Dreamfield coils leaned toward her the way a thirsty thing leans toward water, and the machine forgot the men in grey-green, forgot the purge, forgot the NULL it had been hunting, and heard only the song of the people it had eaten, coming home.

In that instant Sable reached the third node. Her hands moved in the dark of her smock, and the charge went home to the heartbeat of the song.

In that same instant, Devren's knife met the first Enforcer's reader, and the crystal screamed and shattered, and the second Enforcer raised his own reader and read the air, and through the pouring song the reader found what the purge had trained it to find — the one signature that read NULL on every plate, the blank, the girl — and the reader sang the alarm note again, louder, straight at Elara's face.

"Now," Sable said. "Blow them now."

Rook's hand came out of his coat with the last bottle in it, dark and patient, and he looked at it the way a man looks at a coin he is about to spend, and he set it on the gallery rail between himself and the machine, a single dark note among the light. "Then let's make it count," he said. "Three, two —"

The charges blew.

Not together. That was the failure, the single hinge on which everything turned. The third node's charge was still settling in its socket when the first two fired, a heartbeat apart, and the seizure came up the feed-lines wrong — not a clean stop but a wrench, a shudder that ran through the whole chamber like a blow to the spine of a body. The milky light went white, then dark, then white again, and the lattice-stacks screamed, and the coil chamber shook, and dust fell from the high darkness of the ceiling, and somewhere far above them, in a hundred districts, a hundred thousand readers went deaf and came back, deaf and came back, the whole city stuttering on the edge of the blackout they had come to make.

And the third charge, still live in its socket, did not fire.

The Enforcers flooded the gallery. Grey-green at both ends, readers raised, and the alarm note climbed over the ruin of the song, and Elara stood at the rail with the builders' song dying in her throat, and the ten thousand pressed against the inner walls of her mind like a crowd against a gate, and she understood, with a terrible calm, that the hour they had planned for had collapsed into minutes — into seconds — and that the throat was still locked, and the machine was waking, and the only thing standing between her and the full power of the Council was a knife that remembered, a bottle that remembered harder than the world, and a plan that had died in the socket of a charge that had refused to fire.

The coil chamber rang with the alarm.

They had minutes. They had the song. They had each other.

And the machine was waking up around them like a beast in a broken cage.
