chapters.name: The Weeping Stones
chapters.content:
The Stones found them an hour into the country, and they were not what anyone had described.

Sable had said a garden, and so Elara had expected something tended — stones set in patient rows, the way the machine kept its vaults. What the four of them walked into was a field of mourners. The stones stood at every angle, some upright like people waiting, some slumped, some lying on their sides with their faces to the sky, worn smooth as skulls, and every single one of them wept.

The tears ran in the wrong directions. Down the upright faces, yes, but also sideways across the slumped ones, and upward along the lying stones, defying gravity, as if the weeping had no more use for it than the rain had for the earth. Some cried clear water that pooled in their own hollows; some cried a milky grief; some cried nothing but sound — a low, continuous keen, like wind through a pipe, the note Sable had warned about, bending and never resolving. The air was heavy with the sadness of them, and it moved, and it had nowhere to go.

"Keep touching," Sable said. Her voice had gone tight and low. "Keep moving, keep touching, don't stop. Don't look at their faces. Look at the ground between them and walk."

They formed up the way the climb had taught them: Elara in front, Devren behind her with his hand on Rook's belt, Rook hopping between them, Sable last with her hand flat on his shoulder blade. A chain of four, linked by touch, threading through a field of weeping.

The stones were quiet at first. Then the first one reached for Rook.

It was a stone the size of a small house, slumped and round-shouldered, its tears running sideways toward the east, as if it wept for a direction. As the chain came abreast of it, Elara felt the tug through the touch-link, a weight coming off the stone and moving through the air toward the man hopping at her back.

"Rook—"

Too late. His face went slack, his good leg folded, and Devren caught him by the belt and lowered him to the ground. Rook sat on the wet stone floor with his eyes open and gone, his hands gripping his own knees.

"Don't pull him," Sable said, dropping down beside him. "Hold his real hand and let it pass."

Elara knelt and took his hand — the real one, the one in the world, bound in her linen from the trellis fall — and held it, and waited.

---

The exile was a room.

Not a room Rook had ever been in — a small, honey-lit room, a table with a worn cloth, a window onto a street, and a woman with silver in her hair standing at a counter with her back to him, singing. Singing off-key, the way she always did, the way the song went wrong on the high notes and she laughed at herself and went on. A pan on the stove, the smell of bread, rain on a roof that belonged to him.

His whole body knew the room. It was the one he had spent ten years trying to rebuild out of residue bottles and clinking pockets — the one room where he had ever been safe. He knew the woman's voice the way you know your own name. He knew that if she turned around he would see her face for the first time in ten years, and everything would be all right, everything would be home, everything—

She turned. And her face was gone. Not empty — gone, a smooth pale oval where a mother's face should be, and behind it nothing but her song falling into a dark with no bottom. The honey light died, the bread smell went stale and old, the street crumbled into a field of grey weeping stones, and he was standing in the middle of it alone, holding his hands out to a woman who had never turned around and never would, because he had been eight years old when they took her and he had spent the rest of his life trying to carry her back into the world in bottles.

He was not Rook. He was the exile. He was every child who had ever lost a mother to the machine, and he could not remember ever being anyone else, and he could not stop weeping.

Somewhere very far away, a hand held his hand — warm, real, small, a girl's hand that had held a mother's last breath the way he had tried to hold a mother's laugh — and the stone's grief pushed against it, huge and tired, and the girl's hand did not pull. It just held.

Let it pass, said a voice, and the voice was flat and low and it was Sable's, and underneath it, steady as a metronome, was her hand on his shoulder, the fourth link of the chain, still touching, still in the world.

Rook wept. The exile wept through him the way water weeps through a cracked cup, and the hand held, and the shoulder held, and then, slowly, the way a held breath lets go, the exile passed.

He came back with a shudder like a man surfacing from deep water, and laughed — a wrecked, watery sound. "Well. That was my mother's kitchen, the one from the bottle. Only it was somebody else's, and I was somebody else, and neither of us got to keep it."

"It's gone," Sable said gently. "You let it pass."

"It's not gone. It's in here." He touched the clinking coat. "It's always in here. The stone just showed me the whole room at once, and I still couldn't keep it."

"You will," Elara said, the way she had promised a farmer's seven years of love would go home door to door. "When we give it back, you'll keep the real one."

Rook looked at her a long moment, then nodded, and Devren hauled him up by the belt, and the chain re-formed and moved on.

---

They passed ten more stones. Elara watched the chain's edges, felt each pull, steered them wide of the stones that leaned hardest. Some wept for children, some for houses, some for a single word, and the words were all the same underneath — mine, mine, mine, with no one left to answer.

And the Wasteland reached for her.

It happened at a stone the size of a ship, lying on its side, its tears running upward, defying the world. As the chain came abreast of it, Elara felt the tug — not on Rook, not on Sable, not on Devren, but on herself, a slow, vast, patient leaning, like the ground leaning up to meet her boot when she stepped off the shelf of rock. The stone's grief opened like a door, and behind the door was a sound she knew better than her own heartbeat.

The Chorus. Not far and thin now, but close, immense, a million voices holding each other in the dark, singing the question it had aimed at her from the center of the country. And this stone was one of the Chorus's outrunners, one of the oldest, and it reached for her the way the whole country reached — not to take her, not to unmake her, but to know her, to test whether she was what it had waited three hundred years for.

Elara stood still in the middle of the garden, and the exile opened under her feet like a well, and she looked down into it.

It was the Undertow. It was her own alcove on Level Nine, the water-stained walls, the catch-bag, the copper she had scavenged, the rain she had collected in jars. It was Sila humming her forgotten song in the morning. It was Nessa's empty eyes. It was every hollow person she had ever walked past, every taken thing, every discarded life, all of it weeping with nowhere to belong, all of it looking up at her.

And the well said, the way the Chorus said: What are you?

She could have fallen. She could have let it take her the way it had taken Rook — sunk down into that vast, tired, patient grief and become one more voice in it, one more exile with no one to answer, and it would have held her gently, like a familiar hand, and she would have been home in the worst way, the way a drowning man calls the water home.

Instead, she answered.

I'm the girl who carried you, she said. All of you. Ten thousand of you, out of the machine, through the belly of the city, out the other side. I kept your songs in the wards of myself and didn't drop one. I'm Elara Voss, and I'm not here to be taken, and I'm not here to take. I'm here to ask.

The well paused. Ask, it said — a million voices shaped around the single word, three hundred years old — and she understood she was speaking to the whole country, that the garden had gone still around her, that even the upward-running tears had paused in their defiance, listening.

She opened her mouth to speak the question she had come all this way to ask.

But the stone had reached the limit of its tiredness. The pause stretched, then the grief closed like a held breath, and the well shrank and faded, and Elara was standing on the wet floor of the Wasteland with Rook's voice saying her name.

"Bones. Bones, come back. You went somewhere."

She blinked. The garden swam back into focus. She had not moved — she had stood perfectly still in the middle of the path while the whole country leaned in to hear her, and the chain had stopped around her.

"I'm here. It reached for me — not to unmake me. To know me. To ask me what I was."

Sable's face went very still. "And what did you tell it?"

"That I was the girl who carried them. And that I came to ask, not to take." She looked out across the garden, at the stones that had gone quiet. "It wanted to hear it. The whole country leaned in to hear it."

Rook was looking at her with something between awe and grief. "You talked to a stone and it listened."

"It's tired," Elara said. "It's been alone three hundred years. It just wants to know if there's anyone coming."

Sable let out a long breath. "Then we keep going," she said, "while it still knows we're coming for it and not from it. Keep touching, keep moving."

They re-formed the chain, and this time the stones did not reach for any of them. They wept on, patient and tired, and the garden of mourners let them pass like a crowd parting for someone they had been waiting to see.

---

Near the end of the garden, Sable stumbled.

It was a small thing — a stone no bigger than a standing man, hidden among the larger ones, weeping a thin clear grief — and Sable's step hitched as she passed it, and her flat face went briefly, terribly young. A door opened in the memory-smith, a room she had sealed twenty years ago, a face she had never let herself look at directly — the brother she had calibrated the machine for, the one they had taken because she had been good at her work.

"Don't," Sable said, before anyone could move. Her voice was flat again, clamped down. "Don't touch me. Let it pass. I know the rule. I wrote it down for you."

She stood very still, her hand on Rook's shoulder, and Elara watched the exile move through her — watched twenty years of guilt pass across her face in a single held breath — and then it passed, the way everything in the Wasteland passed, because nothing torn out of a person can hold another person forever. It was tired. That was the secret.

Sable opened her eyes. "His name was Maren," she said, very quietly. "I never told you that. I calibrated the machine that took him, and I never said his name out loud in twenty years." She looked at Elara. "When the throat gives back, I want you to know. It wasn't a machine to me. It was my brother."

Elara took her hand — the real hand, the one in the world — and held it. "I'll find him, Sable. He's in here, the way the rest of them are, and when the throat gives back, he'll come home to you."

Sable nodded once, hard, and they walked on.

---

The garden ended the way it had begun: suddenly. One step on weeping stone, the next on bare, scarred ground, and the weight of the air lifted a little, and ahead of them the country opened into a long grey valley, and at the far end, where the valley narrowed and the sky came down to meet the ground, something immense stood in the light, holding a million voices.

The Chorus.

Elara stopped at the edge of the garden, and the chain stopped with her, and she looked at it — at the sound that had been aimed at her all day, for three hundred years — and she felt her mother's breath burn small and warm at the foundation of her, and she was not afraid.

"Rook. Sable. Devren. The Stones are done. This is where I go on alone."

Devren's hand tightened on Rook's belt. "Like hell you do."

"The Chorus unspools living minds," Elara said. "If the four of us go in, it'll have four selves to take apart, and it's been so long since anything new came that it won't remember the difference between a voice and a person." She looked back at them — the farm boy with his father's knife, the ghost trader with his coat of griefs, the memory-smith who had just said her brother's name aloud for the first time in twenty years. "I'm the only one it's been waiting for. I'm the only one who can ask it what it wants."

"Then we wait," Sable said. "Here, at the edge. And if you don't come back—" Her flat voice cracked. "You come back. That's the only rule I'm giving you."

Elara smiled — a real smile, small and bright in the wrong-colored light. "I came all this way to ask it a question. I don't intend to ask it through a locked door."

Rook laughed, wrecked and bright, the sound of a man who had just wept someone else's exile and decided to go on anyway. "Then go ask it, bones. And when it answers, come back and tell us what it said. Door to door, remember? We've got a whole world of doors to knock on."

Elara nodded. She looked at the three of them — her crew, her chain, the people who had carried a girl the machine read as nothing across the belly of the world — and then she turned and walked out of the garden of mourners, across the bare grey ground, toward the place where the sky came down to meet the earth and a million voices held each other in the dark and sang the question they had been singing since before she was born.

Behind her, the Weeping Stones wept on, tired and patient, with nowhere to belong.

Ahead of her, the Chorus waited.

And Elara Voss, who had been nothing for sixteen years and everything for nine days, walked toward the heart of the Wasteland to ask it what it wanted, and the Wasteland leaned in around her like a country holding its breath.
