They walked out of the square together, the wiry limping man in the coat of many clinking pockets and the small fierce woman in the patched green dress, and they did not go far — only to a bench by the old lock-basin, where the water that had once carried the memory barges now carried the reflection of the morning — and they sat down, and she took his hand, and she began to tell him about the beginning.

She told him about the year before he was born, and the roof that leaked, and the song she sang before he was in the world. She told him about the day he was born, and the midwife's name, and the way the light came into the room. She told him about the first time he laughed, and the second, and the third, and how each one had been a different kind of coin and she had kept them all. She told him about his father, who had died in the Fringe when Rook was small, who had taught him to whistle. She told him the stories she had told him at bedtime, the ones that were his, that belonged to him by right of having been a child in her arms.

And Rook sat on the bench with the morning on the water and his mother's hand in his, and he let her give him back his childhood the only way it could be given: not as memory, but as story, freely given and freely received, the way the whole new city was learning to give and receive, door to door, asking first, always.

He still could not remember. He would never remember years six through ten; the machine had burned them, and burned things do not come back. But he had found his beginning, and the beginning was not a set of memories. It was a woman with a silver voice who had kept the laugh and the song and the kitchen safe for thirty years, and who had known him the moment he limped into her square, because a mother's fierce hope does not need a memory to recognize its child. It needs only the shape of the child, and the shape was still there, worn thin in the middle by years of holding, the way Devren's knife was worn thin.

He thought of Elara, who had carried his mother's laugh across the Wasteland and up the spine of the machine and given it back, and of the promise she had kept, door to door. He thought of Sable's door, and Devren's knife, and the boy who was Valerius learning to be a boy. He thought of everything that had come home.

And he thought of the name his mother had given him in the market square, and he said it under his breath, once, to see how it fit. It fit. It had always fit. It had just been waiting for him to come back and claim it.

His mother heard him say it. She smiled, and her smile was the same shape as her laugh, silver and fierce and full of hope.

"There you are," she said. "There's my boy."

And Rook, who had spent ten years buying ghosts and listening for one voice in ten thousand, who had thought his beginning was a thing he had lost and could never find, sat in the morning of the new city with his mother's hand in his and understood that he had never been lost from her, not once, not for a single day of the thirty years she had searched.

He had found his beginning. It was warm, and it was real, and it had been waiting for him all along, singing off-key in a kitchen, holding out both arms like a bird, saying *again, again.*

set.name: Rook
set.description: Wiry ghost trader, copper-colored hair going grey at the temples, coat of many clinking pockets now nearly empty over a grey coil-worker's smock. CURRENT LOCATION: a bench by the old lock-basin at the edge of the market square in the descending city, sitting with his mother — the silver-voiced woman he followed through the crowd. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: his crushed left knee (held by his boot since the scaffold plate bit it) buckled when he went down on it in the square and he now leans on his mother's arm; wrecked-bright, weeping and laughing, whole. He still cannot remember years six through ten — the machine burned them, and burned things do not come back — but he no longer needs to: he has found his beginning, because his mother kept his laugh, his song, and the honey-lit kitchen safe for thirty years, the one copy the machine never found. KNOWLEDGE: everything prior, plus: he followed his mother's returned laugh and off-key song to the market square and found her singing beside a stall of painted cloths; she has been searching for him for years — since the collectors took him — and knew him the moment he limped into her square; she told him his true name — not Rook, the streets' name for a scavenging bird, but the name she gave him over his cradle, which he said back and which fits; she is giving him back his childhood as story (freely given, freely received) since the memory itself is gone; he understands the beginning was never a jar or a ghost or a memory he could buy — it was her, always her, singing off-key in a kitchen. RELATIONSHIPS: his mother (reunited after thirty years; she remembers for both of them and is giving him back his childhood as story), Elara (who carried his mother's laugh and gave it back, door to door, keeping her promise to find her for him), Sable, Devren (blood-bonded). POSSESSIONS: his coat of many clinking pockets, now nearly empty; his true name, given back; his mother's laugh and song, matched at last. GOAL: sit in the morning of the new city with his mother and let her give him back his beginning; to bring her to the crew and to the first morning of the new city (Ch 39).

CURRENT LOCATION: the market square of the descending city — a bench by the old lock-basin where the water that once carried the memory barges now carries the morning's reflection — sitting with her son Rook. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: a small woman in a patched green dress, grey hair coming loose, honey-and-cracked-glass singing voice; weeping and laughing with joy at finding her son; she has been searching for him for years — since the collectors took him — and never stopped; her fierce hope did not die, only got quieter, harder, and more like her. KNOWLEDGE: she kept Rook's laugh, his off-key kitchen song, and the honey-lit kitchen safe in her own head for thirty years — the one copy the machine never found; on the morning of the Descent her own laugh and song came home to her and she understood the machine had given everything back, so she walked the market squares of the descending city for three days, catching the arm of every man with copper hair and asking 'What is your name?', until Rook limped into her square; she remembers his childhood for both of them — his first word, the day he climbed onto the table, the way he said 'again' with both arms out like a bird, the bedtime stories — and is giving them back to him as story, freely given and freely received. Three days after the Descent, Rook followed his mother's returned laugh and off-key honey-lit kitchen song to a market square in the descending city and found her singing on a crate beside a stall of painted cloths. She has been searching for him for years — since the collectors took him — and she knew him the moment he limped into her square; she knelt on the cobbles, put her hands on his face, and said 'You have my laugh. You have my song. You have to be my boy.' She told him his true name (not Rook, the streets' name for a scavenging bird, but the name she gave him over his cradle), and he said it back and it fit. They held each other on the cobbles while the new city's crowd stood in a loose ring around them. She is giving him back his childhood as story: the memory itself is gone — the machine burned years six through ten, and burned things do not come back — but she kept his laugh, his song, and the honey-lit kitchen safe for thirty years, the one copy the machine never found. This fulfills Elara's promise in the ghost-den ('I'll find her for you, Rook') and the return of Chapter 34. Rook still cannot remember his early childhood but no longer needs to: he has found his beginning. They now sit together by the old lock-basin, and Rook carries his true name.

Rook and his mother — the silver-voiced woman — sit together in the new city; he has found his beginning and carries his true name. They may appear together on the first morning of the new city (Ch 39) as a sign of the change the return has made, and Rook may bring his mother to meet Elara.

chapters.name: Enough
chapters.content:
She woke before the bells.

It was the first morning of the new city, and Elara Voss woke in a room that had light in it — a real window, with glass, that opened — and she lay still a moment and let it happen: the light falling across the grey coil-worker's smock folded on the chair, the patched trousers, the rubberized vest, the catch-bag with its small weight of nothing much. Seven mornings since the Descent. Seven mornings since she had stood at the gorge and poured out ten thousand and a million and one and felt the last thread go home.

The first thing she did, every morning now, was reach for the weight.

It was not there. That was what still stopped her breath for half a heartbeat, every time: the vast drowned city of voices that had pressed against the inner walls of her mind, the wards, the streets between the lives, the whole three-hundred-year harvest of the world's stolen pasts — gone. Poured out. She had walked out of the machine's throat and down the wind-posts and into a world that was descending, and the weight had gone with it, the way a held breath goes.

She lay in the light and tested it, the way you test a tooth after the ache is gone, afraid of the ache and afraid of its absence. Empty. She was blank again. The file that had been stamped with zeroes when she was ten was true again, in the only way it had ever been true: there was nothing in her that had been planted, nothing harvested. Sixteen, nearly seventeen, and empty.

And for a moment — the old moment, the one that had followed her all her life through the water-stained Undertow — she felt the old shape of it closing around her. Worthless. A room with nothing in it. A NULL.

And then the warmth.

Deep in the smallest room, in the deepest fold, where no machine had ever reached and nothing had ever been taken, her mother's last breath waited. Warm as a hand. It had been there when she was ten and the readers read NULL and the file was stamped with zeroes. It had been there when Corvin Ash pressed the bolt to her temple and the ten thousand came flooding in. It had been there through the flooded ways and the Wasteland and the wind-posts and the throat of the world — the one thing that had always been hers, the one thing she had never been required to give back, because it had never been taken.

Not much, she thought, the way she had thought it in the emptied throat, standing with the silence closing around her.

Then, the way she had learned: it was everything. It was enough.

She got up, dressed, and walked into the first morning of the new city.

Aethon lay at rest in the harbor of the world, its spires still high but its hull settled into the water and the fields, sky and slum become one city at last. The trellis sea hung slack and sang in the wind. The cloud-sea had become ordinary water, and the morning light lay on it the way light lies on any water that has never been anything but water. The great bells rang the hour, and they were ordinary bells — bells for the market, for the beginning of work, not alarms — and the whole city heard them and went on with its morning.

She walked down through the levels she had grown up in, and they were not dark anymore. The coil-hum that had been the heartbeat of the Undertow was gone; the water-stained walls and crowded alcoves stood open to a light they had never known, and people were doing ordinary things in that light — mending, cooking, arguing, laughing — with their own pasts whole in them.

On Level Nine, in the weaver's block, Elara stopped in a doorway she knew. A woman with pale blue eyes and a shawl of unraveling wool sat by a window that had never had a window, singing. Not humming a forgotten song with nothing behind it — singing, whole, the song the coils had eaten, the first thing the machine gave back. Sila looked up, and she knew Elara, and she did not stop singing; she only smiled around the notes, and the song went on, and Elara stood in the light and listened, and then went on too.

The market square was full of the morning. A bench by the old lock-basin caught her eye — a wiry man in a coat of many clinking pockets, and beside him a small woman in a patched green dress with grey hair coming loose, their hands twined on her knee, the woman talking and the man listening the way you listen to a thing you have waited thirty years to hear.

Rook looked up and saw her. His face did something complicated and bright, and he said something to the woman, and the woman looked at Elara the way people looked at her now — the way you look at a door you have spent your life on the wrong side of — and then Rook was limping toward her, fast as his ruined knee would carry him, and the woman came after him, and Rook said, "Elara. This is my mother."

Elara had known, the way you know a thing the moment it is in front of you, that the laugh she had carried had found its owner. "You found her," she said. "You found the laugh."

"I followed it," Rook said. "Three days. Market squares." He was laughing and not laughing, wrecked-bright. "She's been looking for me for years. Since the collectors took me. She kept the laugh — the one copy the machine never found. Elara, she kept my laugh."

His mother took Elara's hands in both of hers. They were a working woman's hands, warm and dry, and they were shaking. "You carried it," she said. "You carried my laugh across the world and gave it back to him. I have been trying to think of a thing big enough to say to you, and there isn't one. There isn't a word big enough. So I'll just say thank you, and mean it with everything I have."

"You don't thank me," Elara said. "I only carried it. You kept it. Thirty years, you kept it — the machine never found it because it was never in the machine. You're the one who saved it. I promised him in a ghost-den I'd find you for him. I didn't find you. You found him. It was you, all along."

Rook's mother laughed — the silver laugh, out in the open air — and Rook heard it answered in his own chest, where a copy had lived for ten years waiting to be matched, and they matched, and the morning rang with it.

"It's a good morning," Rook said, and he said his true name then, the one his mother had given him over his cradle, saying it to Elara the way you show a friend a key that finally fits. "This is who I was all along. I just didn't know it."

"It fits you," Elara said.

"We're going to the bone-yard this afternoon," Rook said. "I want to show her the Guild — show her Sable, show her the door. You coming?"

"Later," Elara said. "I've got walking to do first. There's a city I've never seen from the outside."

She left them on the bench by the lock-basin, the mother already telling the son the next story of his own beginning, and the morning on the water behind them.

She passed the steps of the old Remembrance Salon, and the doors stood open to the daylight, and on the steps sat a woman in a fine dress gone slightly limp with wearing — the noblewoman from the velvet box, who had once drunk a farmer's love and laughed by evening. She sat with a Steward in a grey smock, hands loose in her lap, talking hesitantly, like a child learning a new language, about the shape of an ordinary day; the Steward listened, and no one was taking anything from her, and she was learning the craft of being only herself.

The bone-yard, when Elara reached it, was a different place from the one she had first been brought to in the dark. The black cloth was gone from the window, and the door stood open to a light it had never known, and the charter was nailed to the jamb, and Elara stood and read it the way you read a scripture in a church you built yourself: no memory taken that is not freely given; no memory given that is not freely received; every life belongs to the living of it.

Sable came out and stood beside her, and they looked at the yard together — the refitted prototype standing in the open, its dark crystal warm in the sun, a Steward settling a thread of someone's grandmother into the hands of a woman who had come asking. Asking first, always.

"Rook found his mother," Sable said.

"I saw. She kept his laugh for thirty years. The machine never got it."

"The machine never got a lot of things." Sable was quiet a moment. "How are you? Truly."

Elara considered the question the way she had considered the weight that morning. "I'm empty," she said. "I poured it all out, and there's nothing left in me but the one small thing. And it's enough. I keep testing it, every morning, waiting for it to not be enough — and it is. It always is."

Sable nodded slowly. "You told me once you were built to hold all of it and give it all back. You did. And the thing that's left —" She touched her own chest, where a boy's song about rain on a tin roof lived now, carried the way Elara carried her mother's breath. "It was never the archive that made you worth something. You knew that before any of us. You just had to live long enough to believe it."

At the freight yard, where the west rim water line met the fields, Devren stood with his peacekeeping force — the young woman from the second service deck, the grey sergeant with the scarred jaw, the purge-captain in his collarless coat — and he was telling the knife's story again, the true one, wheat and rope and bread and the merciful throats of lambs, a thing of carrying never of conquest, and the men and women of the new city's keeping stood in a loose circle and learned it by heart, the way you learn a thing you mean to pass on.

Devren saw Elara and came to her. "You're walking the whole city," he said. "Checking on it."

"Just looking at it. It's the first one I've ever seen from the outside." She looked past him at the Fringe, the fields coming up green where the tithe had once lain on them like frost. "You're looking east again."

"I'm always looking east," he said. "One day I'll walk out there and show the knife to my father's grave and tell him it's done. And then I'll come home." He said home like a man tasting a word he had never been allowed to use. "It's a good morning, Elara."

"It is," she said. "It's the first one."

She went up then, up through the emptied spine of the machine, up the wind-posts to the crown where the throat of the world opened — not to check anything, only because she knew, the way you know where a thing is, that the boy would be there.

He was. He sat at the crystal rim, his back to the emptied throat, watching the morning come up over the city that had once hung beneath his feet. He was only a boy, with his mother's eyes and nothing else left of three hundred years. The extraction blade lay dark and dead at his feet.

Elara sat down beside him, a little way off, and they watched the morning together for a long time.

"I heard it go home," he said at last. His voice was a boy's voice, small and unused. "All of it. Even the first one. I felt it go."

"It did," Elara said. "Every one of them."

Below them the city rang with ordinary bells, and the water lay bright in the harbor, and people moved through their own mornings.

"What do I do now?" he asked.

"Whatever you want," Elara said. "That's the whole of it now. Nobody decides for you. Nobody takes from you. You get to start."

"I don't know how to start. I was never allowed to. I don't even have a name. The machine ate it before I had one."

"Then you get to choose one," Elara said. "That's what the new city is for. That's what a first morning is for." She stood and looked down at him — not with hate, not with forgiveness, but with the plain clear sight of someone who has seen a thing for what it is. "You can start with anything. A name. A place. A life. It won't be the one you were going to have. But it'll be yours."

He looked up at her with his mother's eyes, and something in his face — a door that had been locked so long it had forgotten it was a door — opened a little, and let the morning in.

"Yours," he said, trying the word. "Mine."

She left him there at the rim of the emptied throat, not remade, not finished — started. The way a life starts. The way a city starts. The way a world starts, on a first morning, with ordinary bells.

She walked down the wind-posts and out of the machine and into the city, and the morning was hers the way it was everyone's: freely given, freely received. She walked through streets where people were remembering their own lives, where a boy held a button-eyed bear and a woman sang with a whole voice, where a farmer said his daughter's name to the fields and the fields answered with green.

And at the water's edge, where the old lock-basin had once launched the memory barges and now held only the reflection of the sky, Elara Voss stood alone in the first morning of the new city, and she reached down into herself the way she had done every morning of her life, and there it was.

Her mother's last breath. Warm as a hand. Turning into sunlight.

She had carried the world and given it back. She had held ten thousand and a million and one and opened her hands and let them go home. And the one memory that had always been hers was still there, in the deepest fold, the smallest room, the thing she had kept before she knew what keeping was — the proof that she had never been empty, never been nothing, never been a room with no light in it.

Not much, she thought, one last time.

And then: it was everything. It was enough. It had always been enough. She had just needed to carry the whole world to learn it.

Elara Voss walked into the first morning of the new city, and she was blank, and she was whole, and the warmth at her center went with her — warm as a hand, turning into sunlight — and it was enough.

It was always going to be enough.

set.name: Elara Voss
set.description: Sixteen, nearly seventeen; born blank, now blank again but no longer empty. FINAL STATE: walked into the first morning of the new city (Aethon settled into harbor, sky and slum one city) and found that being blank but not empty is enough — it was always enough. CURRENT LOCATION AT CHAPTER'S END: the water's edge at the old lock-basin, where the memory barges once launched and the water now holds only the reflection of the sky; she spent the morning walking the whole city — Sila's alcove on Level Nine (singing whole with a window that never had a window), the market square (Rook and his mother on the bench, where Rook spoke his true name to her and his mother thanked her), the Salon steps (the noblewoman learning to be only herself with a Steward), the bone-yard (read the Guild charter nailed to the door; told Sable she is empty but it is enough, and Sable told her it was never the archive that made her worth something), the freight yard (Devren telling the knife's true story to the peacekeeping force; he told her he is always looking east and will one day show the knife to his father's grave and then come home), and the crown of the wind-posts at the emptied throat's rim, where she sat with the boy who was Valerius and told him he gets to start, that nobody decides for him anymore, and that he can choose a name. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: whole, at peace; every morning she tests the weight where the archive used to press and finds only the one small warm thing; her throat has healed from singing the counter-frequency. KNOWLEDGE: everything prior, plus: the machine stands empty and clean; the giving-back is complete; the one memory that has always been hers — her mother's last breath, warm as a hand, turning into sunlight — remains in the deepest fold and is enough; she has carried the world and opened her hands, and the proof that she was never nothing was with her before she knew what keeping was. RELATIONSHIPS: the crew (Sable, Devren, Rook — who has found his mother and will bring her to the bone-yard that afternoon), the boy who was Valerius (left at the rim, told he can start), Corvin Ash's charge fulfilled, Sila (who knows her and smiled around the notes), Rook's mother (who took her hands and thanked her). POSSESSIONS: patched trousers, rubberized vest, catch-bag, grey coil-worker's smock, Orrin's song, the builders' work-song, the counter-frequency (sung into the machine and released), and her mother's last breath. GOAL: fulfilled — walk into the first morning of the new city and find that being blank but not empty is enough; it was always enough.

set.name: Sila
set.description: Sixty-three-year-old neighbor of Elara in the Undertow, once a singer; her memories were harvested by high-tithe collectors and returned whole in the Descent. FINAL STATE: on the first morning of the new city she sat by a window in the weaver's block on Level Nine — an alcove that never had a window — and sang, whole, the song the coils had eaten, the first thing the machine gave back; she saw Elara in the doorway and knew her, smiled around the notes, and did not stop singing. Pale blue eyes, shawl of unraveling wool. She is whole and singing; her song is hers again.

set.name: Rook
set.description: Ghost trader, now a man with his true name (given back by his mother in the market square), copper-colored hair going grey at the temples, coat of many clinking pockets nearly empty over a grey coil-worker's smock. FINAL STATE: sat with his mother on a bench by the old lock-basin on the first morning of the new city, her hand twined in his, she giving him back his childhood as story; when Elara passed the square he limped to her and introduced his mother, spoke his true name aloud to Elara ('This is who I was all along'), and said he and his mother are going to the bone-yard that afternoon to see Sable and the Guild. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: wrecked-bright, whole; crushed left knee still held by his boot but he moves through the morning anyway; he still cannot remember years six through ten but no longer needs to — he has found his beginning. KNOWLEDGE: everything prior, plus: his mother kept the laugh, the song, and the kitchen for thirty years, the one copy the machine never found; his mother found him, not the other way around, though Elara told her 'You're the one who saved it — I only carried it.' RELATIONSHIPS: his mother (reunited, giving him back his beginning as story), Elara (who carried the laugh and kept her promise), Sable, Devren (blood-bonded). POSSESSIONS: his coat, now nearly empty; his true name; his mother's laugh and song, matched at last. GOAL: sit in the morning with his mother (done), bring her to the crew and the bone-yard; live his beginning, which is her.

set.name: Sable Vey
set.description: Founder of the Guild of Mnemonic Stewards; former memory-smith, grey hair cut short, late forties, cracked open and whole. FINAL STATE: stood with Elara in the bone-yard yard on the first morning of the new city, the black cloth gone from the window, the door open to light, the charter nailed to the jamb, the refitted prototype warm in the sun with a Steward settling a grandmother's thread into a woman's hands — asking first, always. She told Elara that the thing left at her center was never the archive that made her worth something, that Elara knew it before any of them and only had to live long enough to believe it. KNOWLEDGE: everything prior, plus the Guild's charter, the refitted loom/door, and Maren's song about rain on a tin roof carried in her the way Elara carries her mother's breath. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (she asked 'How are you, truly?' and heard the truth), Rook and his mother (coming to the bone-yard that afternoon), Devren, Maren (home, choosing, his song with her always). POSSESSIONS: the refitted prototype, the charter, Maren's returned song, the craft of the machine turned to giving. GOAL: guide the return door to door, asking first, always — and she has found her peace in the doing.

set.name: Devren
set.description: Deserted Enforcer turned crew, Fringe farm boy, leader of the new city's peacekeeping force of former Enforcers who have accepted their own histories. FINAL STATE: on the first morning of the new city he stood at the freight yard where the west rim water line meets the fields, telling the knife's true story again — wheat, rope, bread, the merciful throats of lambs, a cable cut for friends — to the loose circle of the force (the young woman from the second service deck, the grey sergeant with the scarred jaw, the purge-captain in his collarless coat). When Elara came he told her he is always looking east, that one day he will walk out to the Fringe and show the knife to his father's grave and tell him it's done, and then come home — saying 'home' like a man tasting a word he was never allowed to use. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: quiet, fierce, certain, at peace; bandaged right palm healed; the knife is no longer a riddle. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara, Rook (blood-bonded), Sable, the peacekeeping force learning the knife's story by heart, his father's knife that remembers. POSSESSIONS: his father's knife in the boot-sheath, Fringe knowledge of dead ground and patrol patterns, a coat no longer grey-green. GOAL: keep the peace open-handed while the Guild sorts; pass the knife's true story on; one day walk east to his father's grave and come home.

set.name: Purge-Captain
set.description: Former Enforcer purge-captain of the black collar, now serving under Devren in the peacekeeping force, his black collar torn off and the Council seal cut away. FINAL STATE: stood in the loose circle at the freight yard on the first morning of the new city, learning the knife's true story by heart so he can tell it to the ones who come after. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: a real face with real fear and something like relief still living in it; thirty-one years an Enforcer, now learning to be something else. KNOWLEDGE: the purge he led, Elara as the NULL who walked through his column, the coils reversed, Valerius unmade, the readers that sang grandmothers' lullabies; now learning the knife's story by heart. RELATIONSHIPS: Devren (who shows him every night until he doesn't need to be shown), the peacekeeping force, Elara (whom he faced on the gallery). POSSESSIONS: his coat with the collar and seal cut away. GOAL: find a self beyond the collar, learn the knife's story by heart and carry it forward.

set.name: Rook's Mother
set.description: A woman with a silver voice and a mother's fierce hope. FINAL STATE: sat with her son Rook on a bench by the old lock-basin on the first morning of the new city, giving him back his childhood as story; when Elara came she took Elara's hands in both of hers and thanked her for carrying the laugh across the world, and Elara told her the truth: 'You're the one who saved it. I only carried it. It was you, all along.' She laughed her silver laugh and it was answered in her son's chest, and they matched. She and Rook are going to the bone-yard that afternoon to see the Guild. PHYSICAL/EMOTIONAL STATE: weeping and laughing with joy; whole. KNOWLEDGE: she kept Rook's laugh, his off-key song, and the honey-lit kitchen safe for thirty years, the one copy the machine never found; she searched for him since the collectors took him and found him in the market square. RELATIONSHIPS: Rook, her son, found after thirty years. POSSESSIONS: nothing but the memories she kept and the boy she found. GOAL: be with her son and give him back his beginning as story — done, and continuing.

set.name: Valerius (the boy)
set.description: NO LONGER THE HIGH MEMORIAN. A boy who was the machine's coat for three hundred years and is now only a boy, with his mother's eyes, his lullaby gone home. FINAL STATE: on the first morning of the new city he sat at the crystal rim of the emptied throat at the crown of the wind-posts, the extraction blade dark and dead at his feet, watching the morning come up over the descending city. Elara sat with him; he told her he heard it all go home, even the first one, and asked what he does now. She told him he gets to start, that nobody decides for him and nobody takes from him, that he can choose a name — 'That's what the new city is for. That's what a first morning is for' — and something in his face, a door locked so long it forgot it was a door, opened a little and let the morning in. He tried the word 'Mine.' He was left at the rim not remade, not finished — started, the way a life starts. KNOWLEDGE: the lullaby at his foundation went home with the flood; he has no name and must choose one. RELATIONSHIPS: Elara (who named and unmade him, and who told him he can begin). POSSESSIONS: none but the open door of the machine and the morning. GOAL: begin — choose a name, a place, a life of his own.

set.name: Noblewoman of the Remembrance Salon
set.description: Former customer of the Salon, stripped of her borrowed lives. FINAL STATE: on the first morning of the new city she sat on the steps of the old Remembrance Salon, the doors open to daylight, in a fine dress gone slightly limp with wearing, talking hesitantly with a Steward in a grey smock — learning the craft of being only herself like a child learning a new language, about the shape of an ordinary day; no one is taking anything from her, and she is learning. KNOWLEDGE: the vials can never be refilled; what is left of her is the only thing she has ever truly owned. RELATIONSHIPS: the Guild of Mnemonic Stewards, which walks beside her. GOAL: learn to be only herself, one ordinary day at a time.

On the first morning of the new city, Elara Voss walked the whole city from inside: she stopped in Sila's alcove on Level Nine and heard her singing whole (she knew Elara and smiled around the notes); she saw Rook and his mother on the bench by the old lock-basin, where Rook introduced her and spoke his true name aloud, and his mother thanked Elara for carrying the laugh (Elara insisted the mother saved it, not her); she passed the open doors of the Remembrance Salon where the noblewoman sat with a Steward learning to be only herself; she stood in the bone-yard with Sable and read the Guild charter on the door, telling Sable she is empty but it is enough; she went to the freight yard where Devren told the knife's true story to the peacekeeping force and told her he is always looking east and will one day show the knife to his father's grave and then come home; and she climbed to the crown of the wind-posts and sat with the boy who was Valerius at the emptied throat's rim, telling him he gets to start, that nobody decides for him anymore, and that he can choose a name. She ended at the water's edge at the old lock-basin and found her mother's last breath still warm in the deepest fold — warm as a hand, turning into sunlight — and understood it was enough; it was always enough.

In the seven mornings since the Descent, Elara woke each day in a room with a real window that opened, and each morning she reached for the weight where the archive had pressed — ten thousand and a million and one — and found it gone: she is blank again, the NULL file true again in the only way it was ever true, with nothing planted and nothing harvested. Each morning the old shape of worthlessness closed around her for a moment, and each morning the warmth of her mother's last breath in the deepest fold answered it. She told Sable on the first morning: 'I'm empty. I poured it all out, and there's nothing left in me but the one small thing. And it's enough. I keep testing it, every morning, waiting for it to not be enough — and it is. It always is.' Sable told her it was never the archive that made her worth something; she knew that before any of them and only had to live long enough to believe it.

On the first morning of the new city, Rook brought his mother to meet Elara at the market square: he limped to Elara as fast as his ruined knee would carry him and said 'Elara. This is my mother,' told her he followed the laugh for three days through market squares and that she has been looking for him for years since the collectors took him, and that she kept the laugh — the one copy the machine never found. His mother took Elara's hands and thanked her for carrying the laugh across the world; Elara answered that she only carried it, that the mother saved it by keeping it out of the machine for thirty years, and that she had promised Rook in a ghost-den she would find his mother for him — but the mother found him, and it was her all along. Rook then said his true name to Elara the way you show a friend a key that finally fits, and told her he and his mother are going to the bone-yard that afternoon to see Sable and the Guild.

On the first morning of the new city, Elara climbed to the crown of the wind-posts and sat with the boy who was Valerius at the crystal rim of the emptied throat, the extraction blade dark and dead at his feet. He told her he heard it all go home — even the first one — and asked what he does now. She told him the whole of it now is that nobody decides for him, nobody takes from him; he gets to start, and since the machine ate his name before he had one, he gets to choose one — 'That's what the new city is for. That's what a first morning is for.' Something in his face, a door locked so long it had forgotten it was a door, opened a little and let the morning in, and he tried the word 'Mine.' He was left at the rim not remade, not finished — started, the way a life starts.
